docs.title: §9 rules (1)–(6) and the binding rulings
docs.text:
Three rules enacted 2026-09-12 18:00 review (operator directives of 2026-09-12, 247290d): (1) a slot that commits its item with a clean tree before minute 30 takes the next open item (implementer-run.md step 2 — never on a dirty tree, never an item whose stated dependency has not landed, one outcome commit and one journal entry per item); (2) a step family is capped at four attempts since its last sub-step that landed a gate — a numbered step plus all its lettered sub-steps is one family, relettering does not reset the count, a landed gate does — and at four the family is frozen: a review re-scopes the question as a new numbered step or banks the measured negative, and never queues a fifth letter (this replaces the former "items that fail twice get rescoped" sentence, which never fired); (3) every item below names the status its result can move (daily-review.md rubric element 7) — an item that cannot is not queued; (4) enumerated-chain licence (operator directive 2026-09-18): when the queue is below the floor, the daily review may write and queue, at full rubric grain, any numbered step that the weekly has enumerated in a §10 chain (today: the "step count to a tuned birdcage" list) whose serial prerequisites have landed — the weekly supplied the question and the validation target, the review supplies the execution detail; it may not add, reorder or re-target chain steps, and a step whose target it cannot make assertable is queued as "write the anchor" and returned to the weekly. Families frozen at enactment: WF-6 step 4 (4h–4k since 4g), ANS-4 step 2 (2a‴, 2e, 2f, 2g since 2a″), PORT-14 step 2 (2, 2b–2e; no gate landed) — each carries its ruling in §7.

Binding ruling — sheets and κ (operator, 2026-10-02). Port and lumped-element sheets are exact rectangles; κ is not applied to them (operator ruling 2026-10-02, interactive session). Evidence: on exact-rectangle ports Palace and ours agree to 0.0000 % at matched order and κ falls to ≈ 1.6e-5 / 1.8e-5 (degree 1 / 2, items 159 / 166) against ≈ 1.1e-2 on the old ragged sheets — κ measured the ragged sheet geometry, not the solver; and the κ-corrected copper F-human 32×32 is non-passive (σ_max 1.000002129) where the uncorrected one is passive (0.999993339, item 175). So: (i) every new fixture or step builds its port / RLC / impedance sheets as exact CAD rectangles (OCC faces — leg_sheet_strip_fraction, the longitudinal ring sheets), never a sub-sheet triangulated out of a box; (ii) the κ width correction is off on exact-rectangle sheets (width_correction_kappa=None), with every gate at its existing band — the passivity ceiling stands; (iii) records measured on the old ragged sheets stay valid as records; moving existing fixtures (the ANS-4 / ANS-6 / ANS-7 F-small half-sheets) to exact rectangles is the weekly's to plan, re-recorded under the (1*) licence, no band moved; κ remains available as a diagnostic (a non-zero κ on an exact sheet is a reading, not a correction).

Binding ruling — capacitor ESR (operator, 2026-10-06, interactive session). Every lumped capacitor carries a 0.2 Ω series resistance (ESR): tuning capacitors on ring gaps, and any RLC sheet that models a capacitor. It is frequency-independent and the same on every capacitor. Why: real RF capacitors are lossy. A lossless C overstates the Q of a copper coil, whose own conductor loss is small enough that the capacitor ESR dominates it. (i) Circuit layer: a capacitor termination is Z = r + 1/(jωC) with r = 0.2 Ω. A feed is driven across its gap's (r + C) branch. Uniform r adds r to every mode's eigen-impedance, so C_mode (from Im λ₁) is unchanged and Re λ shifts by r. (ii) In-model: a series-RC sheet impedance carrying the same r and C. (iii) AED: HFSS's Lumped RLC boundary is a parallel R ‖ L ‖ C. A series (r, C) maps exactly at one frequency to R_p = r(1 + Q²), C_p = C·Q²/(1 + Q²), with Q = 1/(ωCr). At 113 pF and 64 MHz, Q ≈ 110, R_p ≈ 2.4 kΩ and C_p is C to 8e-5. Entering 0.2 Ω as the HFSS R shorts the gap. On a sweep, R_p follows 1/f² away from the conversion frequency, so a SPEC names that frequency. Scope: new steps and fixtures. Lossless-C results stay valid as records, labelled lossless. Not a gate change: r never re-reads or rescues a red. H12c's identity question was posed on lossless C and stands as posed. Whether H12c / H9 are re-posed with r (both sides at once) is the 10-07 weekly's decision, together with which in-flight chains and SPECs adopt it (H9, ANS-8 step 2, the ANS SPEC template, an esr_ohm argument on ring_mode_rows and the terminations).

Rule (6), the chain-extension licence (operator directive 2026-10-02, interactive session). Slots consume a weekly's enumerated steps in about two days, then sit idle until the next weekly (09-30 weekly: 17 of 36 slots short of work). The daily review may therefore write the next numbered steps of a live §10 chain toward that chain's stated subgoal and validation target, tagged (daily, date — provisional), at most six per chain between weeklies (raised from three by operator ruling 2026-10-24, interactive session — dashboard W8: twelve idle periods traced to chains at the cap; the dailies' provisional steps have been ratified without reversion), and re-pose blocked steps within the four-attempt family cap. It never sets or moves a band, tolerance, done-when or validation target, never opens a chain, subgoal or phase, and never ratifies its own provisional ruling; the weekly ratifies or reverts (daily-review.md step 6, weekly-review.md step 3).

Rule (5), the backlog lanes (operator directive 2026-09-28, interactive session). The queue ran dry on 09-27 and 09-28 while 60 chunks were open: rule (4) is the only licence, and every enumerated chain sits on one serial critical path gated by xl windows, weekly rulings and operator steps. From 2026-09-28, when the ready chain steps do not reach the floor, the daily review also writes and queues, at full rubric grain (anchor, control, tier by measurement, the status it can move), items from three standing lanes. Each lane item must be independent of the chain critical path, and a review fills the shortfall round-robin across the lanes, not from one:

  • Lane 1 — revalidation. A 🧪 chunk's never-executed test run through the harness with a quantitative assertion (→ ✅, or a recorded negative plus a known-issues entry), or a ⚠️ chunk's placeholder test replaced by an assertion against the real solve (§3: never by loosening it; the ⚠️ no-new-features rule still holds). Today's list (pruned 2026-09-30 10:30 review; closed since 09-28: PORT-7, TH-4, PORT-8, GEO-3, PORT-4, MAT-1, PORT-6, TH-3, POST-2, PORT-5, WF-3, GEO-5): GEO-1/2/4/6/7, GEO-27…32, PORT-2/3/18, OPS-7/8, WF-1/4 (🧪); TH-2 (⚠️; WF-2 ✅ 2026-10-09, §9 item 346, provisional). Every listed member has been examined and rejected, with reasons (docs/planning/reviews/2026-09-29-daily-1800.md §6, …2026-09-30-daily.md §6): the lane's 🧪 / ⚠️ list is exhausted unless the weekly opens new members. What the 10:30 review queued in its place is the same kind of work on other rows: a closing window on the current image for a 🟡 chunk whose steps closed on the old one (POST-3), an audit's unmeasured control (MAT-5 (D′)), and open known-issues entries whose own "Resolves with" a slot can execute. A probe-only chunk (§3: measurement steps are 🧪 until a gate lands) is revalidated by writing its gate.
  • Lane 2 — feature ladder Tier B, released now. TH-16 (symmetry planes), then TH-18 (layered impedance), then TH-5 (radiation boundary) — item 5's table, no longer held behind the conductor lineage's formal closure. Each is gated on its closed form (Jin, cited) before any birdcage use.
  • Lane 3 — Phases 7 and 8 in parallel, and their materials. Phases 7 (implants) and 8 (Pennes bioheat) are open from 2026-09-28 and do not wait for Phase 6; they consume WF-7's SAR and the F-small phantom, not the tuned coil. MAT-3 (Debye / Cole–Cole) and MAT-5 (temperature-dependent σ) join this lane (ladder C3 released). Phase 8 starts at the gel regime — conduction plus a prescribed source, gated on analytic solutions (§10 Phase 8); Phase 7 at parametric implant geometry in the phantom, gated on a closed form or a published measurement. Until the weekly has written the §10 subgoals and §7 chunks for them, the daily may open a Phase 7/8 chunk itself only where the validation target is a closed form or a cited published result, and names it in the dashboard for the weekly to ratify.

A lane item never displaces a ready chain step above it. Slots do not write items, so the lanes work through the reviews: with three dailies a day, each restocks its four-slot interval from chains and lanes, and a slot that still finds the queue drained stops and journals (the EX-57 fallback is exhausted, missing=0). A drain is reported as a 🔴 dashboard item naming the empty lanes — a supply failure, never a reason to cut slots.

docs.title: Implementer run protocol (Opus, scheduled)
docs.text: Run by scripts/automation/implementer-run.sh via cron, twelve times a day, every day — four after each daily review: 04:30 / 06:00 / 07:30 / 09:00 (after 03:00), 12:00 / 13:30 / 15:00 / 16:30 (after 10:30), 19:30 / 21:00 / 22:30 / 00:00 (after 18:00); no 21:00 run on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, the weekly review's window (full schedule restored 2026-09-28, operator directive; canonical crontab scripts/automation/crontab). One run = one attempt at the top "On deck" item in PROJECT_PLAN.md §9, then the next if it commits before minute 30 (step 2). Sessions never overlap: the grid spacing exceeds the 65-minute hard kill, and all runs share one flock. Since 2026-09-12 (operator directive, enacted by the 18:00 daily review) a run that finishes its item early takes the next one — see step 2.

docs.title: Timebox
docs.text: 60 minutes wall clock, externally enforced (the wrapper kills the session at 65). Note the start time immediately; start no new implementation work after minute 45 — the final 15 minutes are for documentation and leaving a clean tree. A second (or later) item may be started only before minute 30, and only from a clean, committed tree (step 2); the minute-45 rule and every per-command ceiling apply to it unchanged. The per-command compute budget is unchanged and non-negotiable: §5.1 tiers, 20-minute hard ceiling per compute command, mpiexec -n 12 max, timeout at the tier ceiling, shared machine. The one exception is an on-deck item the weekly review marked xl (§5.1 XL tier: ≤ 512 GiB / 16 ranks / 14400 s against fem-em-solver-xl, six per week since 2026-09-13, ledger-gated) — run exactly the command it specifies, bring the service up before and stop it after, and never invent an XL run yourself.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Preflight: git status must be clean. If it is not, do no chunk work: append an anomaly entry to docs/testing/attempts.md describing what you found, commit only that, and stop. Confirm the container is Up per CLAUDE.md.

Exception — already-journaled documentation drift. If a prior run's attempts.md anomaly entry already describes this exact dirty tree, you may land it and proceed with chunk work, provided ALL of the following hold (verify each; do not assume): - the current diff is byte-identical to the one the prior entry journaled (same files, same git diff content); - it touches documentation only — nothing under src/, tests/, scripts/, and no §7 status or done-when change in PROJECT_PLAN.md; - the edits are internally consistent and complete (they read as a finished change, not half of one).

Commit the diff by itself first (docs: land dirty tree journaled <UTC timestamp of the anomaly entry>), note in your own attempts.md entry that you landed it and why the conditions held, then continue at step 2. If any condition fails — new or different dirtiness, anything non-documentation, no prior journal entry — the original rule applies unchanged: anomaly entry, commit only that, stop. Never discard or stash a human's edits; landing an already-journaled doc diff is the only permitted action.

Second encounter — park it and proceed. If a prior run's attempts.md anomaly entry already journaled a dirty tree and the tree is still dirty now, the tree is stuck and stopping again just burns the rest of the day's slots. Whatever the diff contains: - commit it as-is to a new branch recovered/<UTC-timestamp> (create the branch, commit there, return to a clean main); - journal in your attempts.md entry what you parked, the branch name, and the timestamp of the prior entry that made this the second encounter; - then continue at step 2 and do chunk work normally.

A launcher's refused record — leak-held on first encounter (weekly ruling 2026-11-07). If the dirty tree is exactly a scheduled xl / xxl window's record left staged by its launcher — the new harness log under docs/testing/logs/, its test-results.md row, one ledger row and a consumed queue file, nothing else — and the launcher's log (logs/automation/*xl-run.log) shows its commit refused by the pre-commit leak hook, do not stop and do not park: apply §9's leak-held rule yourself, on the first encounter. Move the harness log unchanged to the gitignored logs/leak-held/, commit the rest through the hook as chore(<tier>): scheduled <tier> window — <chunk> <date> (log held by the leak guard), journal which line number the hook named (never the token or its digits) and that the daily review reads the held copy, then continue at step 2. Never --no-verify, never edit the checker; a tree that does not match this shape exactly follows the rules above. (Four slots stopped on one such record on 2026-11-07.)

Parking preserves the content — nothing is discarded or stashed, and the branch is recoverable with one git checkout. The first encounter still stops, so a human editing interactively is never interrupted mid-change; only a tree that survived a full slot unattended gets moved. Never delete a recovered/* branch; the daily review disposes of it. 2. Take the FIRST item under "On deck" in §9 that is not marked done or blocked. Do not choose a different item for any reason. The item's brief (operator directive 2026-10-01) is the ### §9 item N section of docs/planning/chunks/<CHUNK>.md that its two-line §9 entry links — read it whole before acting; an older item without a link carries its brief in §9 itself. Mark the item done / blocked in the §9 entry, and append the outcome line under the brief's heading. If every item is done or blocked, fall back to the chunk named in §9's "obvious next entry" sentence, scoped to one run; note in attempts.md that you used the fallback. If that sentence names nothing, append an attempts.md entry saying so and stop.

Then, if the item is done early, take the next one. After an item's outcome commit (step 4) has landed and git status --porcelain is empty, if the clock reads before minute 30 of the slot, return to this step and take the next open item — the same rule, the same order, and it may repeat while the clock allows. Measured 2026-09-11/12: slots were stopping at minutes 5–20 of 60 because one run meant one item, while the compute-safety rationale ("one executor at a time") is satisfied by sequential items just as well. Three guards, all load-bearing: a second item never starts on a dirty tree (the first item's commit is what licenses it — an incomplete first item parks per step 4 and the slot then stops, it does not move on — except a pre-registered negative, operator directive 2026-10-01: if the item's brief carries PREDICTED RED: <assertion> range [a, b] lines, every red assertion is one of them and lands inside its range, and every other assertion is green, the item is parked and journaled exactly as an incomplete item (step 4, outcome blocked, "predicted red, inside range" in the entry), and once main is clean the slot continues under the minute-30 rule; an unpredicted red, a red outside its range, or any other failure stops the slot as before); an item that says "depends on item N landing" is taken only if N's commit is on main; and each item gets its own outcome commit and its own attempts.md entry (step 5), never a merged one. Nothing here changes the ban on concurrent executors or the per-command tier ceilings. 3. Execute the chunk following .claude/agents/implementer.md (read it first) and the chunk's §7 entry, which carries the implementation plan. Specialist executors exist for three chunk classes — an EX-* example chunk goes to example-runner, a measurement-only mesh/resolution probe to mesh-probe, a version-bump record sweep to record-reconciler (.claude/agents/); everything else stays with the implementer agent. plan-navigator and log-pathologist are available read-only for lookups and disputed prior logs. Never spawn auditor on your own closure — auditing is the review's job.

Three rules on spawning, all load-bearing: - Only this repo's agents exist. implementer-run.sh denies every built-in agent type by name, so general-purpose/Explore/Plan are unavailable by construction. Never route chunk execution around the specialist definitions — the executor's prompt is the accumulated trap list, and a generic agent would rediscover them at your expense. - One executor at a time, never concurrent. example-runner and mesh-probe issue compute; two of them in parallel would double-book the 12-core budget the guard hook enforces per-command but cannot enforce across simultaneous sessions. One chunk per run makes this natural — keep it that way. - A delegated chunk is still yours. The executor's report is evidence; you own the commit, the attempts.md entry, and the §4 claim, exactly as if you had run it. If its report and the logs disagree, the logs win. - Running an example: the closing window is the script through the harness (11-02 weekly ruling, PROJECT_PLAN §10; OPS-74; EX-170 … EX-172 closed on it). ./scripts/run_examples.sh is host-side and is not in sandbox.excludedCommands, so a scheduled slot invoking it bare gets permission denied ... docker API from its inner docker compose call (2026-08-29, 08-30, 09-01). Wrapping it in docker compose exec is the other half of the same trap and exits 127 — never do that. The ruling's three clauses:

 1. This, as one bare, whole command, **is the closing window**:

    ```
    scripts/testing/run_and_log.sh <ID> "./scripts/run_examples.sh -e <group>:<n> -n <n> -t <s>"
    ```

    The harness call is sandbox-exempt, so the script's inner
    `docker compose` reaches the socket.
 2. A setup figure needs its own earlier window (with
    `FEM_EM_SETUP_FIGURES=1`) that closes nothing. The closing window
    is the last.
 3. A guide edited after its closing window admits only digits from
    the closing log, or arithmetic on them, and says so ("by arithmetic
    from the log"). A phrase with no log behind it is removed or marked
    "a reading, not measured".

 Always write the selector with its group (`-e mesh:3`, never `-e 3`) —
 hand-built selectors have cost slots. `--dry-run` touches no socket and
 runs fine sandboxed; use it to see the inner command, not as a required
 step. This rule binds a spawned `example-runner` too; say so in its
 spawn prompt.
  • Executors run in the foreground, and their harness windows carry the 660 000 ms timeout. Spawn with run_in_background: false, say in the spawn prompt that the "Never run the harness with run_in_background" rule below binds the executor's own Bash calls (foreground, timeout 660000 ms, container-side timeout -k 30 sized to return a footer), and never end your turn while an executor is in flight: the headless CLI waits at most 600 s for background tasks and then terminates the whole session (Background tasks still running after 600s; terminating), SIGKILLing the executor and any harness window it holds. The 2026-09-01 00:00 slot — the first able to delegate — lost EX-36 leg (mesh) this way: example-runner returned with its third ./run_examples.sh window still running (killed host-side 267 s in, mid-mesh:8, footerless; the container process ran on and wrote artifacts nobody witnessed), the slot "resumed" it and ended its turn, and the session was terminated at minute 19 with no journal, no commit and three untracked logs. A launcher backstop (export CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS=0 in implementer-run.sh, so a slot that backgrounds anyway is bounded by the 65-minute kill rather than the 600 s ceiling) is proposed to the operator, not landed — reviews cannot write scripts/automation/. Until it is, this rule is the only protection.
  • Outcome:
  • Complete (§4-done: verification executed, quantitative assertion, harness log + elapsed time recorded): commit code + tests + logs + §7 status flip together on main, marking the On-deck item done in the same commit. A chunk whose §7 row points to a history file (docs/planning/chunks/<ID>.md, OPS-46) gets its step narrative appended to that file; the status flip and the ≤ 2-sentence state line stay in the row.
  • Incomplete (out of time, or blocked): park ALL code changes on a branch attempt/<CHUNK-ID>-<UTC-timestamp> (commit there, return to a clean main). On main, commit only the attempts.md entry plus any §7 annotation (🟡/🚫 with the blocker named). Never leave main red or dirty — a half-applied change on main costs the next run its preflight.
  • Always append an entry to docs/testing/attempts.md (append-only): UTC timestamp, chunk ID, outcome (complete|incomplete|blocked|anomaly), what was tried, measured numbers, harness log filenames, branch name if parked, and a one-line hypothesis for the next attempt. The daily review is the reader — write for it.

docs.title: Non-negotiables
docs.text:
Everything in .claude/agents/implementer.md applies unchanged: all verification through run_and_log.sh, tier ceilings with kill-and-shrink on overrun, never loosen assertions, rank-safety reductions, no work on ⚠️ subsystems, known-issues.md discipline for unrelated failures.

In tracked Markdown (plan annotations, attempts.md, known-issues, example guides), write "approximately" as ≈, never ~: GFM renders a single ~text~ as strikethrough, so two approximate tildes in one paragraph cross out everything between them (swept 2026-09-28). Literal tildes go in backticks or as \~.

docs.title: Working inside the permission allowlist
docs.text:
Scheduled sessions run against .claude/settings.json with no human to answer prompts — a denied tool call is simply denied. Consequences:

  • All compute goes through scripts/testing/run_and_log.sh ... or docker compose exec ... at the top level of the Bash command. Host python3/pytest are not allowed and the host lacks dolfinx anyway.
  • Never run the harness with run_in_background, and never end your turn while a harness command is running. You are a headless claude -p session: ending the turn exits the CLI (exit 0), which SIGKILLs the backgrounded harness — footerless log, untracked artifacts, no journal entry, and the tree left dirty for the next slot. Three consecutive slots paid this on 2026-08-10/11 (19:30, 22:30, 00:00 — the whole night) on the same item, and a spawned example-runner paid it again on 2026-09-01 00:00 (step 3, fourth rule). Run harness commands in the foreground with the Bash tool's timeout parameter at its 660000 ms maximum, and size the container-side timeout so the command returns a footer inside that window (≤ ≈590 s of container time for a command with ≈1 min of setup). Always write the container-side timeout as timeout -k 30 <s> — a plain TERM does not reliably stop an mpiexec job (MAT-6 step 10, 2026-08-12: timeout 590 fired and the ranks ran on for ≈1 700 s, wedging the container). If a container wedges anyway (exec hangs, restart/kill report "did not receive an exit event"), the recovery is docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d --force-recreate, then verify memory.max and zero stray python3 before continuing. A compute step that cannot finish inside one foreground window at ≤ 12 ranks is too big for a scheduled slot: shrink the case or journal it for the review — do not background it.
  • Read files with the Read/Grep/Glob tools, not cat/sed/head — the generic readers are not allowlisted, deliberately.
  • Multi-line commit messages: use a literal multi-line -m string (a quoted argument containing newlines). The older git commit -F <file> route does not work in scheduled sessions — the 2026-09-01 19:30 slot found Write denied for both $TMPDIR and .git/, so there is no writable target for the message file (corrected by the 2026-09-02 03:00 review; CLAUDE.md's -F advice is for interactive sessions, where Write is available). Command substitution like git commit -m "$(cat ...)" is treated as injection by the permission layer and will be denied.

  • If a genuinely needed command is denied, do not fight it: document the denial in your attempts.md entry so the daily review can propose an allowlist change to the human.

  • AED benchmark numbers are private (CLAUDE.md hard rules): read the gitignored aed_results/ / COMPARISON_private.md / docs/private/ files if you need context, but never copy a number from them into a tracked file, a journal entry or a commit message.

docs.title: Standing execution rules (from §9, moved verbatim 2026-10-24)
docs.text:
Operator ruling 2026-10-24 (interactive session): these blocks used to sit in PROJECT_PLAN §9 above the queue. They bind every slot, every executor a slot spawns, and every review that writes a brief. They keep their letters — "rule (d)", "rule (i)", "rule (j)" cite this section.

⚠️ Standing constraint on the compose allow — read before editing that file. docker-compose.yml line 9 is - ..:/workspace, so write access to it is write access to what the container mounts from the host. The operator granted this knowingly and narrowly (2026-08-22). Edit only environment: keys. Do not touch volumes:, do not add a mount, do not widen a path, and do not change the memory limit (128 G, raised from 64 G by operator directive 2026-08-24) — in this or any future chunk. (The fem-em-solver-xl service added 2026-09-05 is the one operator- authorized exception — a second service with its own 512 G limit under the xl profile; the constraint applies to it verbatim, and chunks do not edit it either. The fem-em-palace service added 2026-09-28 — OPS-61's Palace image, palace profile, the same ..:/workspace mount and 128 G — is the second operator-authorized exception, on the same terms.) A chunk that believes it needs a mount change is a blocked finding for the operator. The Edit(docker/.claude/**) caution stands for the same reason: a nested .claude/ is a settings-override surface. One surviving mechanic: git checkout cannot swap docker/Dockerfile / docker-compose.yml in this sandbox — bind-mounted, "Device or resource busy", a silent wrong-content switch — so any chunk that must move them uses the Edit tool and verifies git status --porcelain.

The docker-socket "runner trap" is diagnosed (fcffa701, operator's interactive session, 2026-09-30): every permission denied … /var/run/docker.sock since 08-29 — slots and spawned executors alike — was a non-bare call: a cd … / date -u; prefix, a ; date / | tail suffix, a pipe or a redirect. Only whole commands matching docker * / scripts/testing/run_and_log.sh * (repo-relative; an absolute path is denied) are sandbox-exempt, and bash_guard.py rule 3 now denies the other shapes before they run. So: every harness call is the whole Bash command; ./run_examples.sh … --dry-run only prints the per-example docker compose exec lines — run each through run_and_log.sh as its own call, never chained with &&. (Old paragraph archived: plan-archive.md § "§9 runner-trap paragraph".)

Standing rules for every item below (from the 10:30 review, kept): (a) an EX-* item may add an additive return key or keyword to a gate fixture's helper it imports, provided the gate module is re-run green through the harness in the same slot and the diff is disclosed; (b) guide artifact references carry the full filename; (c) a src/ change beyond an item's letter follows ruling (a) above — disclosed, its pre-existing gate re-run green in the same slot; (d) (added 2026-09-05 10:30) a slot that parks its item on attempt/*, or otherwise leaves it neither done nor runnable, marks the §9 item BLOCKED with the unblock condition in the same commit as the record — the next slot reads §9 first, and an unmarked item costs it the ten minutes the 09:00 slot spent on e49cb67; (e) (added 2026-09-05 18:00) every negative-control factor in an item is labelled asserted or predicted: asserted only when a prior measurement of the same comparison on the same fixture backs it (cite the log line), predicted otherwise — and a predicted factor is printed beside the measured one, never asserted. An executor that meets a failing pre-registered assertion whose label is missing stops and reports the negative result; it does not decide in-slot (EX-49, 2026-09-05 15:00, ruled by the 18:00 review; MAT-6 step 11, 2026-09-06 07:30, ruled by the 10:30 review); (f) (added 2026-09-06 18:00) a band an item states against an analytic comparand that the executed fixture's own CAD or mesher cannot meet is re-registered by measurement on the same quantity where both sides are the fixture's numbers, said so in the docstring and the journal, and the review ratifies or reverts it (TH-15 step 3a, 16:30 slot — ratified above, ruling (2)); it is never widened silently and never on a quantity that was already green. (g) (added 2026-09-08 10:30) every pytest window below runs with -s — two windows (≈ 9 min) were lost this interval to swallowed prints (TH-15 step 2f, OPS-41), each re-run only because the executor noticed; a log without the readings is a window not spent. (h) (added 2026-09-13 18:00) an executor that re-registers a red anchor's comparand in-slot (TH-15 step 3, 15:00) does so as rule (f) allows only when the new comparand measures the same physics as the old one and says so; a substitute that is true by construction on the fixture (an identity with one side removed by the mesh) is a record, and the item stays at its pre-registered result — red — for the review to rule on. (i) (added 2026-09-13 18:00) the window a step is closed on runs the module as committed: if the module is edited after its last green window (even a comment), the window is re-run before the commit, or the row says it was not. (j) (added 2026-09-14 03:00) a review that writes "Status it can move: X → ✅" first reads X's §7 Done-when and either matches it or amends the row in the same review commit; an executor that meets a mismatch closes on the row (holds 🟡) and flags it, as the 21:00 slot did with TH-14 — the §9 letter never outranks the row.

Every window below that uses §5.1 durable capture copies the idiom verbatim, trailing ; exit $rc included. Since OPS-45 the footer honours a [capture] rc= line only when it is the last output line. Every pytest window runs with -s (rule (g)). Every window runs inside the container through run_and_log.sh — host python3 is denied.

Every item: - The harness call is the whole Bash command: bare, repo-relative, nothing chained or piped. A slot that spawns an executor puts that sentence in the spawn prompt verbatim. - An executor that loses the docker socket mid-item stops and reports. - No edit to a script, test or page after its last window (rule (i)). - Every Bash call that runs a window passes timeout: 660000. Run pytest with -s. Never delete a log. - An item that parks marks itself BLOCKED in the same commit (rule (d)). - A window killed at its tier ceiling is not a result. After a kill, run docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml exec -T fem-em-solver pgrep -c python3 first. - Two heavy windows never run at once. - Read the chunk file's latest "Review ruling(s)" paragraph (the newest dated one; no item is open after the 2026-10-17 18:00 review) before the brief. - Any item that adds lines to WF-14's registry regenerates the API pages and docs/guide/validation.md and runs the page gates in the same slot (WF-1.md, 03:00 ruling Q3; item 394's Wgen / Wval / Wapi / Wdoc windows). - No slot opens docs/private/ or aed_results/. - A smoke-tier (30 s) window puts only tests/environment/test_complex_mode.py on the path, never the full tests/environment (10:30 review ruling, item 364).

docs.title: Weekly planning review protocol (scheduled)
docs.text:
Model: scripts/automation/review-model.env (dated override, self-expiring — see CLAUDE.md § Scheduled automation). High effort.

Run by scripts/automation/weekly-review.sh via cron three times weekly, Monday, Wednesday and Saturday 21:00 local (Monday added 2026-10-02 by operator directive, gaps 48 / 48 / 72 h; full schedule restored 2026-09-28, operator directive; canonical crontab scripts/automation/crontab). Model: Fable 5.1 (REVIEW_MODEL_WEEKLY); the daily reviews run on Opus 5.5. The 21:00 implementer slot is dropped on those evenings, so the session has the window to itself and ends before the 22:30 slot. History: Sunday and Wednesday 02:15 until 2026-09-13 — the Sunday session exhausted the account's 5-hour allowance in ≈20 min on both 09-06 and 09-13 and took the 03:00 review and two slots with it — then Saturday 21:00 only through 2026-09-26 (what the plan calls "the 09-16 weekly" is the 09-19 one). With twelve slots a day draining an enumerated chain list in about two days, each weekly should leave enough slot-executable steps to carry the dailies to the next weekly. One session, documentation work only — no solves, no meshing; reading harness logs is fine.

(Wednesday added 2026-09-01 by operator directive. Reason: the daily review can only queue items whose anchors exist, and several anchors are weekly-owned — on 2026-09-01 that left it honestly two items short and two implementer slots drained. Splitting the interval 3/4 days refills the long-horizon queue mid-week instead of only at the week boundary.)

"This week" means "since the last weekly-review commit", not seven days. Both runs are the same protocol; the interval between them is 3 or 4 days, so step 2's pace arithmetic must divide by the measured elapsed time taken from git log, never by an assumed week. A rate extrapolated from a 3-day window as if it were 7 is exactly the kind of unmeasured estimate the realism rules below delete on sight. Everything else — archive rotation, examples ramp, benchmark commissioning — is interval-driven already and needs no adjustment.

You are the project's long-horizon planner. The division of labour is strict and two-way:

  • You own §1 fidelity, the §6 phase map, §10's long-horizon roadmap (phases, subgoals, dated assessments), examples/ health policy, and Ansys benchmark commissioning and adjudication (§5.4).
  • The daily review owns §7 chunk entries and the §9 On-deck queue. Do not edit §9. Where a subgoal needs implementer work, express it as a §7 chunk (stable ID, §4-compliant done-when) and let the daily review queue it. One carve-out: compressing a closed chunk's §7 narrative into a result block (step 6 below) is weekly-owned hygiene; editing open chunks' status/done-when/plans, and anything in §9, remains the daily review's.

Subagents are available and web tools are not — same economics as the daily review: this session never solves, so subagents cost tokens, not cores. Use them for the read-heavy sweeps (pace measurement, examples audit); keep the judgement calls — what to kill, what to rescope, what a comparison result means — for yourself. Six named agents exist in .claude/agents/ (auditor, log-pathologist, plan-navigator, mesh-probe, example-runner, record-reconciler); during the examples-audit sweep, flag any agent file whose "Last verified against" footer is older than ≈30 days. First review after 2026-09-01: measure agent value — (a) demotion catch rate; (b) pathologist OVERRULED/UNCOUNTABLE rate; (c) review completion vs the 2-of-3-died baseline; (d) navigator citation error count; (e) example-runner closures audited vs implementer-run baseline (the Sonnet-tier experiment). If reviews still die on limits, drop the pathologist to sonnet before other mitigations.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Establish the week. git log since the last docs(plan): weekly review commit (or 7 days if none): chunks/steps closed vs opened, the daily-review commits, growth in docs/testing/test-results.md, attempts parked, known-issues opened/retired.

  2. Measure pace, brutally. Count §4-closed steps this week and attribute each to a §10 phase. Extrapolate the current phase's completion from the measured rate — write the number down even when it is embarrassing, with the arithmetic. No date may appear in §10 without a pace measurement behind it. If the extrapolation says a phase goal is more than \~a quarter away at current pace, that is a scoping problem to fix now (cut the goal, not the honesty).

2b. Progress against cost — one dated section, ending in a decision (added 2026-09-19, operator-approved, from an external code review). Step 2 measures how fast chunks close; this step asks whether the closures, the windows and the slots were worth what they cost, and forces one call. Run

scripts/testing/run_and_log.sh WEEKLY-COUNTS "timeout -k 30 30 python3 scripts/automation/weekly_counts.py"

and read the block from the log it names. (Through the harness because a bare python3 is not on the headless allowlist and would be refused; the log is also the durable record of the counts.) It is read-only, ≈1 s, no solves — counts from the launcher logs, test-results.md, both ledgers, attempts.md, git and (since 2026-09-24) Claude Code's session transcripts for tokens, over the same "since the last weekly-review commit" interval as step 1 (this session's own commits, younger than 12 h, are skipped). Append one section headed ## YYYY-MM-DD to docs/status/weekly-progress.md: the script's block pasted verbatim, then these rows written by you, each ≤ 3 lines and each citing a chunk ID, a log:line or a commit:

  • Newly supported workflows — end-to-end capability a user could now run that they could not last week. "None" is the expected answer most weeks; a closed component gate is not a workflow, and per-workflow parity wording (realism rules below) applies.
  • Uncertainties resolved — questions that now have an answer, including negative ones: a record that says "flat in f", a cost probe that prices a family out, an ANS-* adjudication either way. A negative result that stops work is progress and is listed as such.
  • Defects retired — known-issues entries retired, by name.
  • Repeated failure — anything the script flags with ≥ 2 non-complete entries, plus any chunk that took ≥ 4 entries: say in one line why it keeps costing slots (a wrong estimate, an executor's first pass needing rework, a blocked prerequisite).
  • Lost slots — sessions that did not end ok, with the cause where the log gives one.
  • Cost — the script's compute and session figures stand as printed. Anything it prints as unavailable stays unavailable: never estimate tokens, never back-fill core-hours from memory.
  • Decision — exactly three lines: Continue one activity, Change or stop one activity, and the evidence for each from the rows above. A drained queue or idle slots are never evidence for cutting slots (operator directive 2026-09-28): they are a supply failure, and the change they call for is more enumerated steps or another lane (step 3). If the honest answer is "stop nothing", say what evidence next week would change that. The stop call is carried out through your own instruments — a §10 epitaph, a rescoped subgoal, an xl-pending.md entry superseded — never by editing §9.

No single score, and three numbers are not success: commit count, queue depth (the §9 slot-minutes floor and the XL backlog floor exist to avoid idle windows, not to be filled for their own sake) and machine time spent. Report what each XL / XXL window decided, never how many ran. Keep the section to about a screen; it is a report, not an analytics project — if a row needs a sweep to fill, write "not measured this week" and move on. Commit it on its own as docs(plan): weekly review YYYY-MM-DD — progress vs cost (step 6's commit-first rule).

  1. Audit the roadmap against the mission. Is §10's phase/subgoal structure still the shortest path to §1 (AED-parity for the MRI-safety workflow: construct → tune at 64/128 MHz → drive with saline phantom ± implant → safety quantities; bioheat long-term)? Rescope or kill any subgoal that has not moved in a month. Add subgoals only where a phase lacks a next step concrete enough for the daily review to break down. Keep the §6 phase-map states current. Keep every active §10 chain enumerated at least three open numbered steps ahead (operator directive 2026-09-18): the daily review executes chain steps under §9 rule (4), so a chain with no open numbered step is a week of slots draining into figures. Each chain step names its validation target and its serial prerequisites; the daily supplies the rest.

Ratify or revert the dailies' provisional work (operator directive 2026-10-02, §9 rule (6)). Every §10 step tagged (daily, date — provisional), every daily re-pose and every provisional band ruling since the last weekly: ratify it (drop the tag), revise it, or revert it with a one-line reason. A provisional step that has already landed is ratified or its result re-read; it is never silently kept.

Supply the slots to the next weekly (operator directive 2026-09-28). (i) Keep at least four, preferably five, parallel lanes live — §10 chains plus §9 rule (5)'s backlog lanes (revalidation, Tier B, Phases 7/8) — so that no single serial prerequisite (an xl window, a ruling owed here, an operator step) can empty the queue. (ii) Enumerate enough slot-executable steps to carry the queue to the next weekly, and write the arithmetic: slots per day × measured items per slot × days to the next weekly, against open, unblocked, enumerated steps (on the 2026-09-28 schedule that is roughly 40–60 steps between weeklies; use the measured rate, not this figure; since 2026-10-01 the dailies' floor is 160 measured slot-minutes per four-slot interval, so size supply in measured minutes per item class from the daily journals' class table). State the shortfall if you cannot. (iii) Phases 7 and 8 are open in parallel with Phase 6 (§6, §10): write their subgoals with validation targets and their first numbered steps, and ratify or re-target any lane-3 chunk a daily opened. (iv) Every backlog-lane chunk you touch keeps a done-when concrete enough for the daily to queue its next step without you.

3b. Spend the XL slot, or explicitly do not. §5.1's xl tier (operator directive 2026-09-05) is one run per 7 days at ≤ 512 GiB / 16 ranks / 2 h (since 2026-09-13: 4 h) against fem-em-solver-xl (since 2026-09-13: six per trailing 7 days — nightly —, 02:00 Sun–Fri, plus the xxl tier — 754 GiB / 16 ranks / 8 h, one per trailing 7 days, 02:00 Saturday), and this review is the only thing that decides what runs in them. Since 2026-09-13 (operator directive) the decision and the queueing are split: you pre-register every window you commission in docs/testing/xl-pending.md — tier, chunk and step, the exact XL_COMMAND, the measured price from a priced smaller rung (no window without one, §5.1), the readout, and what each outcome decides — and the daily review, as clerk (daily-review.md step 6b), copies every READY entry into docs/testing/<tier>-queue.d/ (a FIFO the launcher drains one file per night, 2026-09-15) as the ledger budget allows, so all six XL windows and the XXL window can be used in a week you run once. Fill the list to the budget: up to six xl entries and one xxl entry ahead. Since 2026-09-15 the daily review also holds a backlog floor (≥ 4 xl and ≥ 1 xxl ahead) and a narrow licence to fill it with priced-family variants and cost probes (daily-review.md step 6b.4); read what it wrote, keep or supersede it, and own everything outside that licence. Read both ledgers and mark run entries. If nothing is ready for a tier, write "not spent" and why. Never split a window, never carry one over, never let an implementer commission one.

  1. Examples health. ./run_examples.sh --list; for each example, find its most recent verified run in docs/testing/logs/ (or note there is none) and whether its XDMF outputs still reflect current capability. You may not solve — a stale or broken example becomes a §7 chunk with the staleness stated. §5.4's bar is a ramp: an in-progress phase owes min(5, gating chunks closed ✅) clean runnable examples, each demonstrating gated capability from a distinct angle (geometry, materials, drive, or output quantity), XDMF that opens in ParaView; a completed phase owes the full five. Count each phase against its ramp. The daily review enqueues an example chunk after each gate closure (daily-review.md step 5), so a shortfall here means that mechanism missed — open the missing §7 chunks yourself and state the per-phase count and shortfall in the review.

  2. Ansys benchmarks (§5.4), both directions.

  3. Commission: should a new examples/ansys_benchmarks/<case>/ be opened? Yes only when a phase milestone has landed on gated physics since the last case. If yes: write the SPEC.md skeleton (geometry, materials, BCs, ports, frequencies, quantities to export — no judgement calls left to the operator) and a §7 chunk to implement the runnable half. Keep the case small enough that one AED session replicates it. A commissioned case that is ready for the operator to replicate goes at the top of the dashboard's Waiting-on-you list (docs/status/dashboard.md, daily-review.md step 7) — that list is how the operator learns about it.
  4. AED numbers are private (operator directive 2026-09-02). Ansys licence terms restrict disclosure of benchmark results, so they are never in a tracked file: read them from the case's gitignored COMPARISON_private.md / aed_results/ on this box (absent on a fresh clone), write the numeric adjudication to the gitignored docs/private/<case>-adjudication-<date>.md, and put only the qualitative verdict (agree / disagree / inconclusive, and what it decides) into PROJECT_PLAN.md, the dashboard and the commit message — no AED R/X/ΔZ values, tet counts, pass counts, energy errors or timings. A relative agreement level (our-vs-AED difference in %, "within x %") may go public with the verdict (operator ruling 2026-09-24).

  5. Adjudicate: if any case gained AED numbers from the human operator since last week, adjudicate them now — agreements promote into §7 gates with the AED value as the reference; disagreements open a known-issues entry and a diagnosis chunk. A disagreement is a finding, never something to explain away.

  6. Plan hygiene. If PROJECT_PLAN.md exceeds 4,000 lines, or any closed chunk or closed step carries more than ≈50 lines of narrative, move the closed narrative verbatim to docs/planning/plan-archive.md (append, matching its entry-header format and preamble contract — never summarize into the archive), and leave a result block of ≤ 15 lines in §7: status, close date, the gated numbers, log IDs, live carry-forwards, and the archive pointer. Verify zero loss before committing: every removed line must appear verbatim in the archive (a set-difference check over non-blank lines is sufficient), and every § reference in CLAUDE.md and docs/automation/*.md must still resolve. Same treatment for docs/testing/attempts.md: entries older than 7 days move verbatim to docs/testing/attempts-archive.md (was 14 until 2026-09-19: the rotation ran every week and the file was still 1.04 MB / 14 194 lines, because 14 days at ≈12 entries a day is that much — measured, 220 entries. Nothing reads further back than the interval since the last weekly; the archive is one grep away). docs/testing/known-issues.md (added 2026-09-19): every agent is told to check that file before debugging, and two thirds of it was retired entries — 451 KB of 669 KB. Move them out each week, mechanically:

scripts/testing/run_and_log.sh WEEKLY-ROTATE "timeout -k 30 30 python3 scripts/maintenance/rotate_plan_archive.py known-issues YYYY-MM-DD"

(through the harness: a bare python3 is not on the headless allowlist). The tool moves every entry whose heading says RETIRED / RESOLVED / FIXED / CLOSED to docs/testing/known-issues-archive.md, verbatim, runs the zero-loss check itself, and leaves one index line per entry so a grep for a test name still lands. It is a no-op when nothing is retired. A §7 row whose history already moved to docs/planning/chunks/<ID>.md (OPS-46, rotate_plan_archive.py chunks) keeps that file where it is when the chunk closes — closed chunks' files are not rotated into plan-archive.md; this rotation is otherwise unchanged.

§7 row budget (operator directive 2026-10-01): every §7 row ≤ 2 KB. §7 was 726 KB of a 935 KB plan because each row carried its whole step history inline. A row holds its ID, a short title, the status glyph, a ≤ 2-sentence current-state line, its Done-when (the contract the auditor reads) and the tier; everything else lives in docs/planning/chunks/<ID>.md. Each weekly runs the census through the harness (rotate_plan_archive.py chunks --census, lists rows over 2 048 B) and moves every listed row with rotate_plan_archive.py chunks SPEC --date YYYY-MM-DD: one state line per ID (≤ 2 sentences, from the row's latest ruling, no figure the row does not carry) and, where the row states one, a Done-when: line copied verbatim (the tool checks it is a substring of the row). A chunk file that already exists gets the row text appended under a dated heading; the tool checks byte identity either way and writes nothing on a refusal. The 10-03 weekly additionally hand-condenses the rows the 2026-10-01 interactive migration condensed mechanically — a title cell that derived badly (e.g. ANS-7's, which opens with a history pointer) or no Done-when found: rewrite the title to the chunk's short name and lift the done-when from the chunk file. Dailies and slots keep rows in budget as they write: new history goes to the chunk file, the row gets only the glyph and state-line change (implementer-run.md step 4 already says so).

§10 holds the current assessment of each kind, not the series (added 2026-09-19, operator directive; effective from the first weekly after that date — the backlog was moved by the operator's interactive session). §10 had grown to 121 KB because every review appended a new dated block — pace ledger, phase-exit assessment, agent-value measurement, examples health, rulings owed — beneath the old ones, and only the newest of each is current. When you write this week's block of a kind, move the previous block of that kind, verbatim, to docs/planning/plan-archive.md in the same rotation (same zero-loss check; rotate_plan_archive.py history SPEC DATE takes === <label> <first-line> <last-line> spans and leaves the pointer line you give it). §10 then carries: the phase/subgoal structure, the live chains with their open numbered steps, operator directives still in force, epitaphs (one line each, they are the lesson), and one dated block of each assessment kind. A trend across weeks is read from docs/status/weekly-progress.md and the archive, not kept inline.

Commit-first checkpoint (added 2026-08-30). Do the rotation before any other edit in this session and commit it on its own as docs(plan): weekly review YYYY-MM-DD — archive rotation the moment the zero-loss check passes. Then, after each of steps 3–5 lands a file, git add it and amend nothing — commit again as … — <step name> if the step's output is complete, otherwise leave it staged. Reason: the 2026-08-30 02:15 session wrote ≈10 000 lines across seven files between 02:19 and 02:52 and died before its single commit; the dirty tree tripped the 04:30 slot's preflight, was parked by the 06:00 slot, and every implementer slot until the 10:30 daily review found a drained §9 — five implementer slots and two review slots lost to one un-checkpointed session (attempts.md 2026-08-30T09:31Z … T14:00Z). Several small commits are cheaper than that; §5.2's audit-note prohibition is about content-free commits, not about checkpointing real work.

  1. Commit the remainder as docs(plan): weekly review YYYY-MM-DD. If nothing needs changing, commit nothing — §5.2's audit-note prohibition applies here too.

docs.title: Realism rules (the reason this review exists)
docs.text:
• Measured pace or no estimate. Every dated assessment cites the week's closure count and the arithmetic. "On track" without a number is deleted on sight.
  • Per-workflow parity claims only. "Tunes a shielded 8-rung birdcage at 128 MHz to within X of AED" is a claim; "HFSS parity" is not.
  • A goal names its validation target — closed form, published measurement, or AED comparison — or it is not a goal yet, and writing the target is the subgoal.
  • Kill stalled subgoals in writing. A subgoal rescoped or killed gets a dated one-line epitaph in §10 saying why; silent deletion hides the lesson.
  • Do not let scaffolding outrun physics. The ⚠️ backlog came from building features on a proxy (§2). A phase may not open implementation subgoals while its predecessor's validation gate is red. Open is not red: Phases 7 and 8 run in parallel with an open Phase 6 (operator directive 2026-09-28) on their own closed-form or published targets, consuming already-gated inputs (WF-7's SAR, the F-small phantom).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• §9 On deck belongs to the daily review; never edit it here.
  • Never loosen a test bound, a done-when, or a §10 criterion to make history look better.
  • Write "approximately" as ≈, never ~, in any tracked Markdown: GFM renders a single ~text~ as strikethrough, so two approximate tildes in one paragraph cross out everything between them (swept 2026-09-28). Literal tildes go in backticks or as \~; ~~…~~ is for deliberate retractions only.
  • known-issues.md discipline applies.
  • Your session transcript is not durable; anything worth keeping goes into the repo in this session's commit.

docs.title: Backends: DolfinX by default, Palace on request
docs.text:
A backend is the field solver behind a Study. The Study, its YAML file and femem run describe the problem once; the backend turns that description into fields and port quantities.

  • DolfinX (the default). Every gated record in this repository was produced on it. It is the reference, and it is the coupling host: SAR, |B₁⁺|, probes, tuning and the thermal hand-off all read DolfinX fields.
  • Palace (opt-in, for scale). Palace (AWS Labs) is an open-source frequency-domain FEM solver. The package writes a Palace case and reads Palace's port output back; it never imports or links Palace. Today the Palace backend returns the four-port S-matrix of the F-small birdcage, nothing else.

docs.title: The three stages
docs.text:
The Study does not launch Palace. A Palace-backed solve runs in three stages: the Study writes the case, a separate run executes Palace on it, and the same call reads the result back after checking the case's checksum.

From Python, the first call writes the case into case_dir and raises PalaceRunRequired; the exception carries the Palace command and the directory to run it in. Calling solve again with the same case_dir, once Palace has written its output, returns a PalaceStudyResult:

```python palace-backend from mpi4py import MPI

from fem_em_solver.backends.palace import PalaceRunRequired

docs.title: study is a four-port F-small Study (see api/Study.md).
docs.text:
try: result = study.solve(MPI.COMM_WORLD, backend="palace", case_dir="palace_case") except PalaceRunRequired as pending: print(pending.cwd, pending.argv)


From the command line, the same three stages are: `femem run` writes the case
and exits with code 3 ("external run pending"); Palace runs in the case
directory; the same `femem run` reads the output and writes its summary into
the output directory:

```bash palace-backend-cli
femem run tests/package/wf1/f_small_four_port.yaml --output-dir out --backend palace
cd out/palace_case    # run the Palace command below here, on the Palace service
femem run tests/package/wf1/f_small_four_port.yaml --output-dir out --backend palace

The Palace command the package asks for, by default, is:

```text palace-command palace -np 8 case.json


`Study.solve(..., palace_ranks=N)` changes the rank count in that command.

## What is refused, and why

- **A parallel communicator.** The Palace backend writes and reads on one rank;
  `Study.solve(backend="palace")` on more than one rank raises. Palace's own
  parallelism is the rank count in its command.
- **A missing `case_dir`**, an unknown backend name, and any geometry,
  conductor, excitation or element degree the writer does not support (only
  the gapped four-port birdcage with lumped ports, degree 1 or 2) raise before
  anything is written.
- **An edited case.** The writer never overwrites a case file. If a file in
  `case_dir` differs from what today's writer would produce, the call raises
  `FileExistsError` naming the file, so Palace output is never read against a
  case it was not computed on.
- **`--backend palace` with `--ranks` or `--estimate`** on `femem run`.
- **A study file asking for an output Palace has no route for.** On
  `femem run --backend palace`, the `outputs.sar`, `outputs.b1_plus` and
  `outputs.probes` sections, a `tune:` section, `study.sweep_hz` and a
  `thermal:` section are each refused by name, as are a `conductor:` and
  `capacitor_sheets` excitation. The error names the key; nothing is
  dropped silently.
- **A study the Palace writer cannot take, on the command line.** On
  `femem run --backend palace`, a hole-wall birdcage (`geometry.as_hole`) and
  a launch on more than one rank are refused by name with exit code 2, before
  any mesh is built and before anything is written. An element degree other
  than 1 or 2 is refused when the file is read (`study.degree`). The checks
  are in `tests/package/test_arch1_u79_palace_inputs.py`.
- **Launching Palace from the `Study`.** Palace lives in its own container
  image, and the solver container has no Docker socket. A `Study` that starts
  Palace itself would need either Palace inside the solver image or a socket
  mount; both are deployment decisions, not package code.

## What the Palace backend carries

The YAML route honours one `outputs` key and returns one result; the lists
below are the code's own (`tests/package/test_arch1_u76_palace_outputs.py`
compares them with `fem_em_solver.study_yaml`):

```text palace-outputs
honoured: outputs.directory
returns: s_matrix
refused: outputs.b1_plus outputs.probes outputs.sar study.sweep_hz thermal tune conductor capacitor_sheets

femem run --backend palace refuses every other output by name, with exit code 2, before anything is written.

docs.title: The binding condition
docs.text: Every Palace-backed result names a reduced cross-check at matched element order on a shared mesh against the DolfinX backend. A Palace number without that cross-check is not a result of this package.

docs.title: The cross-check of record
docs.text:
The Palace backend is held to the same input giving the same answer. On the ×1 exact-strip F-small birdcage at 64 MHz, the S-matrix read back through Study.solve (degree 2) and through femem run (degree 1) must equal the recorded Palace read of the same case, Frobenius-relative, within the tolerance below (rendered from LEG_D0_REPRODUCTION_BAND and checked by tests/package/test_wf17_backends_page.py). The degree-2 read also ties per class to our own degree-2 DolfinX record, and must differ from Palace's degree-1 read, so the read is not blind to the case.

text palace-tolerance Frobenius-relative S tolerance: 1e-09

The nodes that hold it:

  • tests/package/test_arch1_palace_backend.py::test_u16_backend_refusals — the refusals above.
  • tests/package/test_arch1_palace_backend.py::test_u16_case_equals_ops61 — the written case equals the matched-order Palace inputs of record (config keys; mesh byte for byte).
  • tests/package/test_arch1_palace_backend.py::test_u16_read_path_on_recorded_output — the reader on recorded Palace output.
  • tests/package/test_arch1_palace_backend.py::test_u16_palace_read_back — the degree-2 read back through Study.solve, the tie and the order control.
  • tests/package/test_arch1_palace_backend.py::test_u16_cli_read_path_on_recorded_output — the CLI reader on recorded Palace output.
  • tests/package/test_arch1_palace_backend.py::test_u16_cli_palace_read_back — the degree-1 read back through femem run.

They are registered under Study and run_study_file on the validation-envelope page; see also the API pages for Study and run_study_file. The matched-order Palace comparison these nodes reproduce is the public "Palace at matched order" section of ans:4's comparison.

Not claimed: a Study that launches Palace, any output other than S, any fixture other than the F-small birdcage, or accuracy beyond the cross-check above.

docs.title: Capacitor sheets with ESR from YAML on the copper F-small birdcage
What you will compute
docs.text: The same study as capacitor sheets with ESR, written as a study file instead of Python: the F-small four-port birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1) around its saline phantom, with its rings and legs cut out of the mesh and carrying a Leontovich surface impedance for copper. One leg port, P2, is replaced in the model by a series R–C sheet, a capacitor with its equivalent series resistance (ESR). The remaining sheets stay lumped ports and are driven in turn, so the study's S-matrix is 3×3 over P1, P3 and P4. The whole study runs through one call, fem_em_solver.run_study_file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks; the block below takes ≈ 1 min. The study file is f_small_copper_capacitors_esr.yaml; the block reads it by its repository path, so run it from the repository root.

docs.title: The study file
docs.text: ```yaml capacitor-esr-yaml

docs.title: WF-17 step 15 (§9 item 627): f_small_copper.yaml with one 0.2 ohm ESR capacitor sheet on P2; record: WF-17 step 14's (U84) gated per-sheet circuit-reduction identity.
docs.text:
femem: 1 study: frequency_hz: 64000000.0 degree: 1 geometry: kind: four_port_birdcage preset: f_small as_hole: true material: sigma: 0.5 epsilon_r: 78.0 excitation: kind: capacitor_sheets c_f: 6.629e-11 esr_ohm: 0.2 sheets: [P2] conductor: kind: leontovich sigma_s_per_m: 58000000.0


The `excitation:` section is `capacitor_sheets`: `c_f` in farads, `esr_ohm`
in ohms, and `sheets`, the port ids whose sheets become capacitors. The key is
`sheets`, not `on`: YAML reads a bare `on` as `true`, so the loader refuses it.
Everything else is the copper file of
[copper rings from YAML](copper_birdcage_from_yaml.md).

## Run it

```python capacitor-esr-run
from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("tests/package/wf1/f_small_copper_capacitors_esr.yaml")
print(run.summary["kept_ports"], run.summary["capacitors"])

A capacitor-sheet study writes no Touchstone file: the JSON summary carries the reduced S-matrix over kept_ports and a capacitors block.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
The run's 3×3 S-matrix equals the circuit reduction of the unterminated 4×4 (every sheet a 50 Ω lumped port) with Z = r + 1/(jωC) terminating P2, to the first band below. The unterminated 4×4 itself ties to the degree-1 copper record (relative distance of its self / adjacent / opposite class means) to the second. The bands, and the resistance on the sheet, are:

text capacitor-esr-yaml-bands Study S vs the circuit reduction with Z = r + 1/(jωC): 1e-03 Unterminated 4×4 vs the copper record: 1e-09 Series resistance r (Ω): 2e-01

The test, not the block, computes the readings from the run and checks them against these bands. The same file with esr_ohm: 0.4 misses the 0.2 Ω reduction; the test runs that control itself, which shows the ESR in the file reaches the solve.

docs.title: Capacitor sheets with ESR on the copper F-small birdcage
What you will compute
docs.text: The F-small four-port birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1) around its saline phantom, with its rings and legs cut out of the mesh and carrying a Leontovich surface impedance for copper. One leg port, P2, is replaced in the model by a series R–C sheet: a capacitor with its equivalent series resistance (ESR). The remaining sheets stay lumped ports and are driven in turn, so the study's S-matrix is 3×3 over P1, P3 and P4. Everything is built from Python with one Study and one CapacitorSheets excitation.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks; the block below takes ≈ 1 min.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The block builds the study, solves it, and prints the kept ports and the sheet's impedance Z = r + 1/(jωC).

```python capacitor-esr from fem_em_solver import (CapacitorSheets, FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LeontovichWall, Study) from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

study = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True, strip_fraction=0.5), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), CapacitorSheets(6.629e-11, esr_ohm=0.2, on=("P2",)), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, conductor=LeontovichWall(5.8e7), ) result = study.solve() print([p.port_id for p in result.port_definitions], result.capacitor_impedance_ohm)


`CapacitorSheets(c_f, esr_ohm, on)` takes the capacitance in farads, the
series resistance in ohms and the port ids whose sheets become capacitors; the
other sheets keep the lumped-port drive. The capacitance is an input here, not
a tuning result.

## What you should see

The study's 3×3 S-matrix equals the circuit reduction of the unterminated 4×4
(every sheet a 50 Ω lumped port) with Z = r + 1/(jωC) terminating P2, to the
first band below. The unterminated 4×4 itself ties to the degree-1 copper
record (relative distance of its self / adjacent / opposite class means) to
the second. The bands, and the resistance on the sheet, are:

```text capacitor-esr-bands
Study S vs the circuit reduction with Z = r + 1/(jωC): 1e-03
Unterminated 4×4 vs the copper record: 1e-09
Series resistance r (Ω): 2e-01

The test, not the block, computes the readings from the solved study and checks them against these bands. The same study with the resistance doubled on P2 misses the 0.2 Ω reduction; the test runs that control itself, which shows the ESR reaches the solve.

docs.title: Why every capacitor carries 0.2 Ω
docs.text:
Real RF capacitors are lossy. A lossless capacitor overstates the Q of a copper coil, whose own conductor loss is small enough that the capacitor's ESR dominates it. The project therefore puts r = 0.2 Ω on every capacitor in new studies; lossless results stay only as labelled records. A uniform r adds r to every mode's eigen-impedance, so the mode capacitance C_mode is unchanged.

On the human-scale copper birdcage the same ESR is applied at the circuit layer instead of as an in-model sheet: tuned copper birdcage. The four-port S-matrix without capacitors is on four-port S.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• More than one capacitor sheet (the three-sheet route is printed, not asserted, in the gate).
  • A tuned capacitance: c_f is an input.
  • A resonance, match, Q or R_in statement.
  • The power identity with the sheet's dissipation counted (gated in WF-16 step 10, not re-run here).
  • Degree 2.
  • Capacitor sheets on the human-scale birdcage (refused).
  • The YAML route: the file tests/package/wf1/f_small_hole_pec_capacitors.yaml is lossless and on the perfectly conducting hole wall, not on copper.
  • Any external-solver comparison.

docs.title: Clinical-scale body-coil fixtures (F-clinical 1.5 T / 3 T)
docs.text: This page collects the geometry of the two clinical-scale birdcage fixtures of GEO-38 (PROJECT_PLAN §10 chain C), the sources each number comes from, and the rulings that fixed the modelling choices. Every number in the geometry table below is checked against the code by tests/package/test_geo38_clinical_fixture_page.py, and every number in the heating section by tests/package/test_wf17_clinical_heating_page.py, and every number in the rod-in-box section by tests/package/test_wf17_clinical_rod_records_page.py, and every number in the closed-form gel-box section by tests/package/test_wf17_clinical_closed_form_records_page.py.

docs.title: What the two fixtures are
docs.text:
F-clinical-1.5T (64 MHz) and F-clinical-3T (128 MHz) are nominal clinical body-coil geometries, not scanner models: 32-leg high-pass birdcages inside a closed PEC can, with the ASTM F2182 gel box as the load. F-clinical is the production fixture for new human-scale work; the Phase 6 exit stays on F-human (PROJECT_PLAN §10, the clinical-scale coil fixtures paragraph).

Both are built by the same generator. The 3 T table is derived from the 1.5 T table by overriding five values (rung diameter, rung span, leg spacing, shield radius, air padding); everything else is inherited.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Lengths in metres unless marked. "Record" rows are version-tagged measured values ((1*) licence), not bands.

Quantity F-clinical-1.5T F-clinical-3T frequency 64 MHz 128 MHz legs 32 32 ring-gap sheets (port census) 64 64 rung (conductor) diameter 0.710 m 0.704 m RF shield diameter 0.745 m 0.743 m shield (can) length 0.954 m 0.700 m rung length (ring-centreline separation) 0.450 m 0.516 m leg span 0.5143 m 0.5800 m ring gap (arc) 17.14 mm 17.14 mm leg width / ring tube radius 12 mm / 4 mm 12 mm / 4 mm leg-box section 4 × 4 × 21.43 mm 4 × 4 × 21.43 mm leg-box corner clearance to the can 5.685 mm 7.685 mm load ASTM F2182 box 650 × 420 × 90 mm, 650 mm on the axis, centred (C2); C1 stand-in cylinder 0.10969 m × 0.65 m, volume-matched ASTM F2182 box as at 1.5 T (C8 box window); C8 r1 / r2 on the same stand-in cylinder sizing rungs (resolution, conductor_resolution r1 / r2) 0.015 m, 1.6 mm / 2.4 mm 0.015 m, 1.6 mm / 2.4 mm cells r1 / r2 (records) 1 147 366 / 912 804 1 057 895 / 808 126 U₁ / U₂ at r1 (records) 1 525 193 / 7 885 674 1 425 765 / 7 335 988 gmsh at r1 (measured) 295.1 s, -n 2, 2026-10-15 12:07 CDT (20261015T170721Z_GEO-38-s1a-W1-r1-a2.log) 286.5 s, -n 2, 2026-10-18 12:04 CDT (20261018T170415Z_GEO-38-C8-W1-r1.log)

Notes on the rows:

  • Shield (can) length is not a typed parameter. The generator places the can at ±z_extent with z_extent = max(coil_length/2, leg_spacing/2 + ring_minor_radius, phantom_height/2) + air_padding; the 3 T table computes its air_padding so that the can is the sourced 0.70 m.
  • Rung length at 3 T (review ruling (b), 2026-10-18 03:00): the sourced 0.58 m is the leg span (coil_length), asserted at 1e-9; the ring-centreline separation keeps the 1.5 T absolute leg overhang (0.0321428571 m past each ring), so it reads 0.516 m. The 1.5 T convention (sourced 0.45 m = ring-centreline separation, leg span 0.5143 m) is not carried over.
  • Box cells. With the ASTM box in place: 1.5 T 1 149 150 cells at -n 1 / 2 / 4 (C2, 20261015T185056Z_GEO-38-s2-W3-n4.log); 3 T 1 061 517 cells at -n 1 / 2 / 4 (C8b -n 1, 20261019T172435Z_GEO-38-C8b-W1-box-n1.log; C8b -n 2, 20261019T173044Z_GEO-38-C8b-W2-box-n2.log; C8 -n 4, 20261018T171406Z_GEO-38-C8-W3-box-n4.log).
  • Can-cap clearance at 3 T (review ruling (c)): the box ends sit 25 mm from the can caps; the closed can stays, and the clearance is named for the weekly.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
The three sources found 2026-10-14 (docs/planning/chunks/GEO-38.md, "Nominal geometry"):

  • https://mri-q.com/uploads/3/4/5/7/34572113/body_coil_distriubtion_mrm.20177.pdf — "Efficient high-frequency body coil for high-field MRI" (MRM): the 3 T high-pass quadrature body coil, 58 cm long, 70.4 cm in diameter, inside a shield 74.3 cm in diameter and 70 cm long. Supplies the 3 T rung diameter, shield diameter, shield length and rung length.
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12137786/ — a 70 cm-bore 3 T scanner modelled with a 32-rung high-pass birdcage. Supplies the leg count (32) and the high-pass topology.
  • https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11442125 — US patent 11 442 125: 1.5 T rungs 45 cm long on a carrier of 65 cm inner diameter, the RF shield within ≈ 2 cm of the end-ring diameter. Supplies the 1.5 T rung length and the shield-to-ring spacing.

Modelling choices, not sourced:

  • the 1.5 T rung diameter 0.710 m, set just outside the 0.70 m patient space rather than at the patent's 65 cm carrier;
  • the 1.5 T shield length, which follows from the air-padding rule (padding = (0.03/0.07) · ring_radius) rather than from a source;
  • the leg overhang past each ring (0.0321428571 m);
  • the leg-box section (4 × 4 × 21.43 mm);
  • the closed PEC can itself (a modelling stand-in for the RF shield);
  • the 3 T rung-length reading (0.58 m as the leg span, ruling (b)).

The weekly may refine a value only with a cited source (PROJECT_PLAN §10).

docs.title: The rulings
docs.text:
• The human operator's port-census ruling (2026-10-15): 32 legs ⇒ every ring gap of both rings is a lumped sheet, 64 sheets and a 64×64 untuned S-matrix; tuning and SAR by two ports in quadrature with the 64 gaps as series-RC sheets at the 0.2 Ω ESR; 16 legs considered and rejected because it contradicts the cited 32-rung source.
  • The 2026-10-15 03:00 review's provisional choices: rung length = the ring-centreline separation; the shield as a closed PEC can (new keyword-only shield_radius); F-human's absolute conductor sizing; C1's load a volume-matched gel cylinder; the leg-box dy cut to 4 mm.
  • The 2026-10-15 10:30 corner ruling: leg-box dx 4 mm; the design corner clearance ≥ 5 mm; the shield_radius refusal computes the leg-box corner radius over the actual box azimuths; shield_radius is refused together with leg_gap_length.
  • All of the above ratified by the 2026-10-17 weekly.
  • The 2026-10-15 18:00 ruling concerns the build cache for the C1 (b) column (-n 4 build, column alone at -n 8), not geometry.
  • Item 518's rulings (2026-10-18 03:00 review): (b) the 3 T rung length is the weekly's 0.58 m, asserted at 1e-9 on the rung (leg) span, the chosen parameter (coil_length) printed; (c) the closed PEC can stays and the 25 mm cap-to-box clearance is printed and named for the weekly.

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text:
The 1.5 T table is the single source of truth; the 3 T table is a derived dict. Both are passed to MeshGenerator.birdcage_port_domain, whose keyword-only shield_radius adds the closed PEC can and whose phantom_box places the ASTM box as tag 3.

F_CLINICAL_3T_KWARGS    tests/validation/test_geo38_f_clinical_3t.py
MeshGenerator.birdcage_port_domain(..., shield_radius=..., phantom_box=...)

                        tests/validation/test_geo38_f_clinical_box.py     (C2)
                        tests/validation/test_geo38_f_clinical_3t.py      (C8)

The meshing example that builds the 1.5 T fixture with the box is the mesh:15 guide.

Temperatures are in K per accepted watt.

Field, sense c* θ(t*) at c* P1 +y wall P2 -y wall 1.5 T, ccw (-0.105, 0.0, -0.05) 1.611905088e-03 +4.445002899e-03 +4.110246040e-03 1.5 T, cw (-0.105, 0.0, -0.05) 1.266521350e-03 +3.070816668e-03 +3.262978681e-03 3 T, ccw (0.105, 0.0, 0.05) 6.516151132e-03 +1.272564088e-02 +1.213484346e-02 3 T, cw (0.105, 0.0, 0.05) 5.749650374e-03 +1.042249186e-02 +1.076902943e-02 3 T / 1.5 T, ccw each its own 4.042515e+00 not read not read 3 T / 1.5 T, cw each its own 4.539718e+00 not read not read

  • 20 °C baseline. The window also prints a cem43 per accepted watt; it is the unheated 20 °C baseline, not a dose per watt (a thermal dose is nonlinear in power), so no cem43 figure is quoted here.

docs.title: Closed-form gel-box records (MAT-21 steps 48 / 49)
docs.text:
The numbers below are printed by 20261112T120219Z_MAT-21-P88-W1.log (MAT-21 step 48), 20261112T182020Z_MAT-21-P89-W1b.log (MAT-21 step 49) and 20261110T103343Z_MAT-21-P83-W1.log (the power share), beside the three ratios GEO-38 C39 printed in 20261111T103024Z_GEO-38-C39-W1.log.

Step 48 heats the gel ball by a deposited power P_dep and compares the thermal-dose excess over the unheated baseline with its linear term:

P_dep (W) excess / D0 excess / linear term − 1 0.1 2.38132e-04 1.6194e-04 1 2.38479e-03 1.6212e-03 10 2.41996e-02 1.6392e-02 100 2.81864e-01 1.8384e-01

The excess per watt at 100 W is 1.1836 times that at 0.1 W, so no single number per watt carries it.

Step 49 places the 18-ball lattice at C6's points, weighted by entries 52 / 58's SAR10g, and predicts the 3 T / 1.5 T lever as the power share times SP, the ratio of θ at each field's own c* per deposited watt:

Quantity Value SP 1.1041889 power share (3 T / 1.5 T) 3.6935 predicted lever = share × SP 4.078321 C39 ccw point 4.042515e+00 C39 ccw ball 4.030354e+00 C39 cw point (cw heated at ccw's c*) 4.539718e+00

Step 49's printed verdict reads "lattice resolves the excess"; the planning review reads it. The question it answers is set out in the mat:42 example.

  • Closed form. No FEM field enters either record.
  • Not the clinical SAR. The 18-ball lattice at C6's points, weighted by entries 52 / 58's SAR10g, is a stand-in, not a fit.

  • 1.5 T gel constants. Both records use the 1.5 T gel values.

docs.title: Copper rings from YAML: the F-small four-port with a Leontovich conductor
What you will compute
docs.text: The F-small four-port birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1) around its saline phantom, with its rings and legs cut out of the mesh (as_hole: true). The cut surfaces carry a Leontovich surface impedance for copper instead of a perfect conductor. The study is solved at 64 MHz, one port at a time, and the output is the 4×4 S-matrix in a Touchstone file plus the JSON summary. The whole study runs through one call, fem_em_solver.run_study_file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks; the block below takes ≈ 1 min. Copy the study file next to your script: f_small_copper.yaml.

docs.title: The study file

File What it sets Summary keys it adds Record it carries f_small_copper.yaml conductor: {kind: leontovich, sigma_s_per_m} on the hole geometry (geometry.as_hole: true) of the four-port birdcage conductor WF-1 step 4: the S-matrix class means reproduce the ANS-6 degree-1 copper record

A conductor needs geometry.as_hole: true, is refused on the sphere, and is refused together with study.sweep_hz and with --backend palace; each refusal names the field it refuses.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The block runs the file and prints the conductor section of the summary and the name of the Touchstone file it wrote.

```python copper-yaml from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("f_small_copper.yaml", output_dir="femem_out/f_small_copper") print(run.summary["conductor"], run.paths["touchstone"].name)


The same run from the command line:

```bash copper-yaml-cli
femem run f_small_copper.yaml --output-dir femem_out/f_small_copper

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
The S-matrix class means (self, adjacent, opposite) against the degree-1 copper record (relative distance per class), and the reciprocity, passivity and class-spread gates on the run's own S-matrix. The bands are:

The test, not the block, computes the readings from the run and checks them against these bands. The same file without its conductor: section (a perfectly conducting hole wall) misses the copper record; the test runs that control itself.
