docs.title: A dispersive medium: mean SAR in a Cole–Cole sphere
What you will compute
docs.text:
The mean specific absorption rate (SAR) in the same 1 cm-radius sphere as Your first study, in the same imposed, uniform 1 V/m field at 64 MHz, but filled with a dispersive medium: a two-pole Cole–Cole permittivity with an ionic conductivity,

ε̂(ω) = ε∞ + Σₖ Δεₖ / (1 + (jωτₖ)^(1 − αₖ)) + σᵢ / (jωε₀).

The medium is a ColeColeMaterial handed to Study in place of a fixed (σ, εᵣ) pair. The numbers below are an illustrative two-pole medium, not a tissue.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The fem-em-solver Docker service must be up (docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d), and you work inside it with the repository at /workspace.
  • The solve is complex-valued: switch the container shell to the complex DolfinX build first with source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode. Real mode raises.
  • Cost: ≈ 5 min wall time on 2 MPI ranks, the same mesh and degree-2 solve as the first study.

docs.title: The dispersive study
docs.text:
```python dispersive-sphere import math

from fem_em_solver import QuasiStaticSphereField, SphereInBoxGeometry, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import ColeColeMaterial

R = 0.01 # sphere radius, m

geometry = SphereInBoxGeometry( sphere_radius=R, box_half_width=0.02, resolution_sphere=R / 10, resolution_far=R / 5, sphere_tag=1, ) medium = ColeColeMaterial( epsilon_inf=4.0, poles=( # (delta_eps, tau s, alpha) (50.0, 1.0 / (2.0 * math.pi * 100e6), 0.30), (4000.0, 1.0 / (2.0 * math.pi * 1e6), 0.35), ), sigma_ionic=0.2, # S/m ) field = QuasiStaticSphereField(e0=1.0) # 1 V/m, along z

study = Study(geometry, medium, field, frequency_hz=64e6) print( f"resolved at 64 MHz: sigma = {study.material.sigma:.6g} S/m, " f"epsilon_r = {study.material.epsilon_r:.6g}" ) sar = study.mean_sar() print(f"mean SAR = {sar['mean_sar_w_per_kg']:.6e} W/kg")


## Run it

Save the block as a Python script and run it inside the container, in complex
mode, on 2 ranks (`<script>` is the file you saved):

```bash
source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode
PYTHONPATH=/workspace/src mpiexec -n 2 python3 <script>

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
text dispersive-sphere-output resolved at 64 MHz: sigma = 1.0098 S/m, epsilon_r = 181.279 mean SAR = 3.986757e-08 W/kg

The closed form for a lossy sphere in a uniform quasi-static field, evaluated at the resolved pair, is 3.985081e-08 W/kg, 0.04 % away.

docs.title: Why the medium is resolved at the solve frequency
docs.text: A time-harmonic solve runs at one frequency, so the Study evaluates ε̂ once, at frequency_hz, and solves with the real pair σ_eff = −ωε₀ Im ε̂ and εᵣ = Re ε̂ — here 1.0098 S/m and 181.279, far from σᵢ = 0.2 S/m and ε∞ = 4 because both poles still contribute at 64 MHz. Two shortcuts give a different answer: dropping the Cole–Cole broadening (αₖ = 0, a Debye medium) or dropping the poles (σᵢ and ε∞ alone) puts the closed-form SAR more than 60 % away from the Cole–Cole one, and the test below holds the page's SAR away from the Debye one. A sweep over frequency resolves the medium afresh at each frequency; this page solves at one.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text: No tissue table: the Gabriel parameters are a separate, operator-held step. No coil or port study: a ColeColeMaterial on a port geometry is refused with a TypeError before any mesh. No YAML: this medium is Python-only here.

docs.title: How this page is tested
docs.text: The block above is extracted from this page verbatim and executed through the logging harness by test_wf17_dispersive_sphere_tutorial.py; it must reproduce the record of test_wf15_study_cole_cole.py at every digit that record carries, stay inside the closed-form band, and miss the Debye-reduced closed form.

docs.title: Duty-cycled heating and a container wall on the gel ball
What you will compute
docs.text: The transient temperature rise of a gel ball cooled through its surface by a heat-transfer coefficient (a Robin condition) and heated by a uniform volumetric source that a duty cycle switches on and off. Time stepping is Crank–Nicolson with a Rannacher start-up (two backward-Euler half steps). Then the same ball, with the source left on, inside a container wall whose conductivity and heat capacity differ from the gel's. The wall carries no source, and the cooling acts on its outer surface.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the real DolfinX build: do not source dolfinx-complex-mode, because a thermal-only study has no complex solve. Run with 2 MPI ranks. Each block below takes ≈ 1 min.

docs.title: A duty-cycled source
docs.text:
The block builds a ball of radius 0.1 m and gives it a uniform source of 2000 W/m³, gel conductivity 0.6 W/(m·K), a surface coefficient of 10 W/(m²·K) to 20 °C air, and the gel's volumetric heat capacity. The source is on for the first half of every 1200 s period, and the run takes 94 steps of 150 s.

```python duty-python from fem_em_solver import ( DutyCycle, RobinCooling, Study, ThermalBallGeometry, TransientSpec, UniformHeatSource, )

study = Study(ThermalBallGeometry(0.1, 0.005), None, UniformHeatSource(2000.0)) result = study.temperature( RobinCooling(0.6, 10.0, 20.0), transient=TransientSpec(150.0, 94, 4.18e6), duty=DutyCycle(1200.0, 0.5), )


## A container wall

The block puts the same gel ball inside a wall that reaches out to a radius
of 0.11 m, with conductivity 0.19 W/(m·K) and volumetric heat capacity
1.7e6 J/(m³·K). The run takes 40 Crank–Nicolson steps. Their total is one
fifth of the gel's diffusion time a²ρc/k.

```python wall-python
from fem_em_solver import (
    ContainerWall,
    RobinCooling,
    Study,
    ThermalBallGeometry,
    TransientSpec,
    UniformHeatSource,
)

wall = ContainerWall(0.11 - 0.1, 0.19, 1.7e6)
study = Study(ThermalBallGeometry(0.1, 0.005, wall=wall), None, UniformHeatSource(2000.0))
result = study.temperature(
    RobinCooling(0.6, 10.0, 20.0),
    transient=TransientSpec(348.3333333333334, 40, 4.18e6),
)

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Each block binds study and result:

  • result.temperature is the temperature at the final time, a P1 field on result.mesh.
  • result.max_balance_residual is the largest discrete energy-balance residual over the steps.
  • result.source_multipliers lists the schedule's on/off multiplier for each step and start-up half step. It is empty when no duty cycle is given.

The page states no temperature, error or residual. The test checks the values against the recorded closed-form comparisons.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• A coil or another electromagnetic source; see temperature.md for the imposed-field route.
  • Perfusion, or any tissue.
  • The same studies from a file: thermal_ball_duty_a.yaml and thermal_ball_wall.yaml, gated by test_wf1_yaml_thermal_ball.py.
  • A CEM43 thermal dose.
  • Any external-solver comparison.

docs.title: Estimating memory and time before a solve
What you will compute
docs.text: For one study file: the mesh it builds and the number of unknowns its function space carries, plus a predicted peak memory and wall time for the solve at the current launch width. Nothing is solved; the mesh and the function space are built and then discarded.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks; each block below takes ≈ 1 min (the mesh is built, the solve is not). Copy the study file next to your script: f_small_four_port.yaml.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The block loads the study file and asks for its estimate on the ranks the script was launched with.

```python estimate-python from mpi4py import MPI from fem_em_solver import load_study

study = load_study("f_small_four_port.yaml") est = study.estimate(MPI.COMM_WORLD) print(est.cells, est.unknowns, est.degree, est.ranks)


The same estimate from the command line:

```bash estimate-cli
mpiexec -n 2 femem run --estimate f_small_four_port.yaml

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
The estimate carries these fields, in this order:

text estimate-fields cells unknowns degree ranks predicted_peak_gib predicted_seconds rows_used not_priced

The command line prints one name: value line per field, on rank 0 only. The test, not the page, checks the values against the recorded mesh and unknown counts.

docs.title: What the estimate is built from
docs.text: The prices come from measured solves. For each element degree a power law is fitted to those measurements: peak memory against the unknown count, and wall time multiplied by the rank count against the unknown count. The predicted time is then divided by the current launch width. A study at a degree with fewer than two measured solves is refused by name, and so is a thermal-only study, which has no electromagnetic solve to price. --ranks together with --estimate is refused, because the estimate prices the width the command was launched with.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• How accurate an estimate is on a study unlike the measured solves; the leave-one-out bracket is the gate in test_wf13_study_estimate.py.
  • Degree 2 on this file.
  • Human-scale studies (priced; see test_wf13_estimate_f_human.py).
  • The Palace backend (refused with --estimate).
  • Any external-solver comparison.

docs.title: Estimating a human-scale study before you solve it
What you will compute
docs.text: For the copper F-human birdcage study file: the mesh it builds and the number of unknowns its function space carries, at element degree 1 and at element degree 2, plus the predicted peak memory and wall time of each electromagnetic solve at the current launch width. Nothing is solved; the mesh and the function space are built and then discarded.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks. The human-scale mesh is large: building it takes ≈ 1–2 min at 2 ranks, and each block below builds it once. Copy the study file next to your script: f_human_hole_copper_tune.yaml.

The F-small version of this page is Estimating memory and time before a solve; it explains the fields of the estimate.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The first block prices the study file as it is, at degree 1.

```python estimate-f-human-d1 from mpi4py import MPI from fem_em_solver import load_study

study = load_study("f_human_hole_copper_tune.yaml") est = study.estimate(MPI.COMM_WORLD) print(est.cells, est.unknowns, est.degree, est.rows_used, est.not_priced)


The second block writes a copy of the same file with the one line
`  degree: 1` changed to `  degree: 2`, and prices the copy.

```python estimate-f-human-d2
from pathlib import Path

from mpi4py import MPI
from fem_em_solver import load_study

comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
copy = Path("f_human_hole_copper_tune_d2.yaml")
if comm.rank == 0:
    lines = Path("f_human_hole_copper_tune.yaml").read_text().splitlines(keepends=True)
    hits = [i for i, line in enumerate(lines) if line.rstrip("\n") == "  degree: 1"]
    assert len(hits) == 1
    lines[hits[0]] = "  degree: 2\n"
    copy.write_text("".join(lines))
comm.Barrier()

study = load_study(copy)
est = study.estimate(comm)
print(est.cells, est.unknowns, est.degree, est.rows_used, est.not_priced)

The same estimate from the command line, on either file:

```bash estimate-f-human-cli mpiexec -n 2 femem run --estimate f_human_hole_copper_tune.yaml


`--ranks` together with `--estimate` is refused: the estimate prices the width
the command was launched with.

## What you should see

Each block prints the cell count, the unknown count, the degree, the measured
rows the price was fitted from, and what is not priced. The two blocks build
the same mesh, so the cell counts agree; the degree-2 unknown count is larger.
The test, not the page, checks the values against the recorded human-scale
mesh and unknown counts and against the measured row each degree is priced
from. The predicted seconds and peak memory are the price table's fit, not a
measurement: no 2-rank human-scale solve exists to compare them against.

## The clinical coil at degree 2

The 0.70 m bore clinical birdcage at 1.5 T is priced differently: no mesh is
built, and the numbers are read from one measured run, not fitted. Copy its
study file next to your script:
[f_clinical_15t.yaml](../../tests/package/wf13/f_clinical_15t.yaml). This block
writes a copy at degree 2, in the same way as the block above, and prices it in
seconds at any width.

```python estimate-f-clinical-d2
from pathlib import Path

from mpi4py import MPI
from fem_em_solver import load_study

comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD
copy = Path("f_clinical_15t_d2.yaml")
if comm.rank == 0:
    lines = Path("f_clinical_15t.yaml").read_text().splitlines(keepends=True)
    hits = [i for i, line in enumerate(lines) if line.rstrip("\n") == "  degree: 1"]
    assert len(hits) == 1
    lines[hits[0]] = "  degree: 2\n"
    copy.write_text("".join(lines))
comm.Barrier()

study = load_study(copy)
est = study.estimate(comm)
print(est.cells, est.unknowns, est.degree, est.ranks, est.predicted_seconds,
      est.predicted_peak_gib, est.rows_used, est.not_priced)

The block prints the cell count, the unknown count, the degree, the 16 ranks the row was measured at, its seconds with the mesh build excluded, its peak memory, the row's name and what is not priced. femem run --estimate prints the same on the copy. Without --estimate, femem run refuses the copy before any mesh and names the tier a solve needs: xl for a root grid of up to 3 nodes, xxl for a column set.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:

  • How accurate the prediction is at 2 ranks; the leave-one-out checks are in test_wf13_estimate_f_human.py and test_wf13_estimate_f_human_d2.py.
  • The thermal transient of a human-scale study (stated as not priced).
  • Any output (SAR, B1+) of the human-scale geometry: those are refused on it.
  • Any external-solver comparison.

docs.title: Your first study: mean SAR in a gelled-saline sphere
What you will compute
docs.text: The mean specific absorption rate (SAR) in a 1 cm-radius gelled-saline sphere (σ = 0.57 S/m, εᵣ = 78) sitting in an imposed, uniform 1 V/m field at 64 MHz (the 1.5 T Larmor frequency). The package composes the geometry, the material, the imposed field, a degree-2 time-harmonic solve and the SAR integral behind one object, Study. The answer has a closed form, so you can check it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The fem-em-solver Docker service must be up (docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d), and you work inside it with the repository at /workspace.
  • The solve is complex-valued: switch the container shell to the complex DolfinX build first with source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode. Real mode raises.
  • Cost: ≈ 5 min wall time and ≈ 20 GiB of RAM summed over 2 MPI ranks.

docs.title: The first study
docs.text:
```python first-study from fem_em_solver import ( GelledSalinePhantomMaterial, QuasiStaticSphereField, SphereInBoxGeometry, Study, )

R = 0.01 # sphere radius, m

geometry = SphereInBoxGeometry( sphere_radius=R, box_half_width=0.02, resolution_sphere=R / 10, resolution_far=R / 5, sphere_tag=1, ) material = GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.57, 78.0, 64e6) # sigma S/m, eps_r, Hz field = QuasiStaticSphereField(e0=1.0) # 1 V/m, along z

study = Study(geometry, material, field, frequency_hz=64e6) sar = study.mean_sar() print(f"mean SAR = {sar['mean_sar_w_per_kg']:.10e} W/kg")


## Run it

Save the block as a Python script and run it inside the container, in complex
mode, on 2 ranks (`<script>` is the file you saved):

```bash
source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode
PYTHONPATH=/workspace/src mpiexec -n 2 python3 <script>

docs.title: Four-port outputs from Python: 10 g SAR, |B₁⁺| and a frequency sweep
What you will compute
docs.text: The F-small four-port birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1, 64 MHz) around its saline phantom, driven one port at a time at 1 V, built as a Study in Python rather than from a study file. Three blocks read three outputs from it: Study.sar gives the 10 g mass-averaged SAR in a ball at one centre per port, placed on a ring at each solved port sheet's azimuth; Study.b1_plus and Study.b1_plus_at give |B₁⁺| at listed points; and Study.solve_sweep solves the S-matrix at 10, 64 and 128 MHz on one mesh. The same outputs from a study file are on Four-port EM outputs from YAML and A frequency sweep from YAML.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks. The SAR block takes ≈ 2 min; the other two ≈ 1 min each. Each block is a complete script.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The SAR block solves the S-matrix first, so it can read the solved sheets' azimuths from the result and put one centre per port at radius 15 mm on its port's azimuth. Study.sar then solves the four port drives once more, keeping their fields, and returns one SAR record per drive per centre.

```python sar-python import numpy as np

from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

study = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry.f_small(), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, ) result = study.solve() centres = [ (0.015 * np.cos(np.radians(s["azimuth_deg"])), 0.015 * np.sin(np.radians(s["azimuth_deg"])), 0.0) for s in result.sheets ] sar = study.sar(mass_g=10.0, centres=centres) print(sorted(sar), [len(per_centre) for per_centre in sar.values()])


`Study.b1_plus` projects each drive's magnetic flux density onto a continuous
field once; `Study.b1_plus_at` evaluates `|B₁⁺| = |B_x + jB_y|/2` from it at
the points you give, on every rank.

```python b1-python
from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study
from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

study = Study(
    FourPortBirdcageGeometry.f_small(),
    GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6),
    LumpedPortDrive(),
    frequency_hz=64.0e6,
    degree=1,
)
maps = study.b1_plus()
b1 = study.b1_plus_at([(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)])
print(sorted(maps), {port: bool(valid.all()) for port, (_, valid) in b1.items()})

Study.solve_sweep meshes once and solves the 4×4 S-matrix at each frequency; the phantom keeps its σ and ε_r at every frequency.

```python sweep-python from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

study = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry.f_small(), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, ) sweep = study.solve_sweep([10.0e6, 64.0e6, 128.0e6]) print([float(f) for f in sweep.frequencies_hz], sweep.s_matrices.shape)


## What you should see

The C4 symmetry of the birdcage, read from each Study. The 10 g SAR at port
k's own centre under port k's drive is compared cyclically between
neighbours; `|B₁⁺|` under ports 2, 4 and 3 on a point set rotated by +Δ, −Δ
and 2Δ (Δ the port spacing) is compared with port 1 on the unrotated set; and
each S-matrix, the 64 MHz one and the three swept ones, is compared with the
project's degree-1 record at that frequency. The test, not the blocks,
computes these comparisons; the pairing reads the solved sheets' azimuths,
not the port names. The bands they are held to:

```text four-port-python-bands
S vs the P1 records, per frequency: 1e-09
10 g C4 cyclic pairs: 5e-02
|B1+| C4 covariance: 5e-02

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text: These are per-1 V port-drive records, not absolute or compliance SAR or |B₁⁺|; there is no spatial-peak search and no homogeneity figure. The sweep holds the phantom's 64 MHz σ and ε_r at every frequency. Degree 1 only; the coil is the solid σ = 800 S/m conductor, not copper (a Study with a conductor is refused by solve_sweep); no Touchstone file is written here (the YAML sweep page writes one); no F-human; no external-solver comparison.

docs.title: Four-port EM outputs from YAML: 10 g SAR, |B₁⁺| and point probes
What you will compute
docs.text: The F-small four-port birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1, 64 MHz) around its saline phantom, driven one port at a time at 1 V. From the one field-keeping solve the file's outputs share, a study file can ask for three readings per port drive: the 10 g mass-averaged SAR in a ball at one centre per port (the {ring_radius_m: r} form puts each centre at radius r on its port's azimuth), |B₁⁺| at listed points, and point SAR and |E| at listed points inside the phantom. Each file runs through one call, fem_em_solver.run_study_file, which writes the JSON summary (and the Touchstone file of the S-matrix) next to the results.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks; each block below takes ≈ 2 min. Copy the two study files next to your script: f_small_sar_b1.yaml and f_small_em_probes.yaml.

docs.title: The study files
docs.text:
File What it sets Summary keys it adds Record it carries f_small_sar_b1.yaml outputs.sar (10 g, centres on a ring) and outputs.b1_plus (listed points) sar, b1_plus WF-1 step 5 (item 344): the 10 g C4 cyclic pairs and the |B₁⁺| C4 covariance f_small_em_probes.yaml outputs.probes (five points in the phantom) probes WF-1 step 20 (U70): the summary is point_sar on the run's own fields

Probe points outside the phantom are refused, because the σ and ρ that turn |E| into SAR are the phantom's. On this family probes takes {points: […]}; on the thermal files it takes a list of balls instead.

docs.title: Run them
docs.text:
Each block runs one file and prints which port drives its summary holds.

```python four-port-sar-b1 from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("f_small_sar_b1.yaml", output_dir="femem_out/f_small_sar_b1") print(sorted(run.summary["sar"]["values"])) print(sorted(run.summary["b1_plus"]["values"]))


```python four-port-probes
from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("f_small_em_probes.yaml", output_dir="femem_out/f_small_em_probes")
print(sorted(run.summary["probes"]["values"]))

femem check reads a file without solving it. Two malformed files show what a refusal looks like; each exits with status 2 and names the field it refuses (malformed_sar_mass_zero.yaml names outputs.sar.mass_g; malformed_sar_on_sphere.yaml names outputs.sar, because SAR outputs need a port study):

```bash four-port-check femem check malformed_sar_mass_zero.yaml femem check malformed_sar_on_sphere.yaml


## What you should see

The C4 symmetry of the birdcage, read from the run. The 10 g SAR at port k's
own centre under port k's drive, compared cyclically between neighbours; and
`|B₁⁺|` under ports 2, 4 and 3 on a point set rotated by +Δ, −Δ and 2Δ (Δ the
port spacing), against port 1 on the unrotated set. The test, not the block,
computes these from the run; the pairing reads the solved sheets' azimuths,
not the port names.

```text four-port-records
10 g C4 cyclic pairs (%): 0.8702 3.5284 2.0337 4.5024
|B1+| C4 covariance (%): 1.8695 1.9494 1.6405

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text: These are per-1 V port-drive records, not absolute or compliance SAR or |B₁⁺|; there is no spatial-peak search and no homogeneity figure. Degree 1 only (the degree-2 record is a wider-rank record and is not run here); the coil is the solid σ = 800 S/m conductor, not copper; no F-human; no external-solver comparison.

docs.title: Four-port S-parameters of a small birdcage
What you will compute
docs.text: The 4×4 scattering matrix S of the F-small four-leg birdcage at 64 MHz, with a gelled-saline phantom (σ = 0.5 S/m, εᵣ = 78) inside it. Each of the four legs carries one lumped port on an exact rectangular sheet; every port is driven in turn and terminated in 50 Ω otherwise. One object, Study, composes the geometry, the material, the port drive and the time-harmonic sweep, and returns S and Z.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The fem-em-solver Docker service must be up (docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d), and you work inside it with the repository at /workspace.
  • The solve is complex-valued: switch the container shell to the complex DolfinX build first with source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode.
  • Cost: ≈ 1 min wall time on 2 MPI ranks.
  • Set degree=1. Study defaults to degree 2, which on this coil needs ≈ 8 ranks; the recorded S below is the degree-1 matrix on 2 ranks.

docs.title: The study
docs.text:
```python four-port-s from fem_em_solver import ( FourPortBirdcageGeometry, GelledSalinePhantomMaterial, LumpedPortDrive, Study, )

geometry = FourPortBirdcageGeometry.f_small() # exact port rectangles phantom = GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64e6) # sigma S/m, eps_r, Hz drive = LumpedPortDrive() # 50 ohm on every port

study = Study(geometry, phantom, drive, frequency_hz=64e6, degree=1) result = study.solve() s = result.s_matrix # 4 x 4 complex, port order P1..P4 print(f"|S11| = {abs(s[0, 0]):.4f}") print(f"|S21| = {abs(s[1, 0]):.4f}")


`result.z_matrix` holds Z, and `result.write_touchstone(path)` writes a
Touchstone file of S (pass a path of your choosing).

## Run it

Save the block as a Python script and run it inside the container, in complex
mode, on 2 ranks (`<script>` is the file you saved):

```bash
source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode
PYTHONPATH=/workspace/src mpiexec -n 2 python3 <script>

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
text four-port-s-output |S11| = 0.5901 |S21| = 0.4230

The full matrix reproduces the recorded degree-1 S to ≈ 1e-10 relative (the test holds it to 1e-9). By the coil's four-fold symmetry the other diagonal entries match |S11| and the other adjacent-port entries match |S21|.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text: No tuning, no resonance and no absolute S₁₁ accuracy claim: this is one mesh at degree 1, and S here is checked against its own record and against reciprocity / passivity / symmetry identities elsewhere, not against an external solver at this degree.

docs.text: The block above is extracted from this page verbatim and executed through the logging harness by test_wf17_more_tutorials.py; its S must reproduce the degree-1 record of test_wf16_study_four_port.py to 1e-9 relative.

docs.title: Heating the gel sphere from YAML: temperature rise and probes
What you will compute
docs.text: A gelled-saline sphere sits in an imposed quasi-static 64 MHz field. The field solve gives the SAR inside the sphere; scaled by source_scale, that SAR is the heat source of a steady conduction solve on the sphere's own submesh, with the sphere surface Robin-cooled to the ambient temperature. The output is the temperature rise and the power balance in the JSON summary. The second file adds ball-averaged temperature probes. Each file runs through one call, fem_em_solver.run_study_file. For the same study from Python, see the same study from Python.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode; the field solve is complex) and 2 MPI ranks; each block below takes ≈ 30 s. Copy both study files next to your script: sphere_mat10_thermal.yaml and sphere_mat10_probes.yaml.

docs.title: The study files
docs.text:
File What it sets Summary keys it adds Record it carries sphere_mat10_thermal.yaml thermal: {k_w_per_m_k, h_w_per_m2_k, t_inf_c, source_scale} on the sphere in its box temperature WF-1 step 3: MAT-10's SAR-to-heat record through the file sphere_mat10_probes.yaml the same thermal: section plus outputs.probes (ball centres and radii) probes WF-1 step 6: the whole-ball probe identity

Probes need a thermal: section, and a probe radius must be positive; each refusal names the field it refuses.

docs.title: Temperature rise
docs.text:
The block runs the thermal file and prints the temperature section of the summary.

```python sphere-heating from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("sphere_mat10_thermal.yaml", output_dir="femem_out/sphere_mat10_thermal") print(run.summary["temperature"])


## Temperature probes

The block runs the probes file and prints the ball-averaged temperature rise
of each probe.

```python sphere-probes
from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("sphere_mat10_probes.yaml", output_dir="femem_out/sphere_mat10_probes")
print(run.summary["probes"]["values_k"])

The same heating run from the command line:

```bash sphere-heating-cli femem run sphere_mat10_thermal.yaml --output-dir femem_out/sphere_mat10_thermal


## What you should see

The temperature section of the summary has three keys, in this order:

```text sphere-heating-keys
source_power_w
convected_power_w
theta_max_k

The interior temperature rise is compared with the closed-form steady solution for the uniform-sphere SAR, both for the field-driven source and for the closed-form source solved directly on the same submesh; the source power on the submesh is compared with the field's dissipated power; and the whole-sphere probe is compared with the volume mean of the temperature rise. The bands are:

text sphere-heating-bands Interior error vs the closed form: 1.1e-01 Interior error, direct P1 comparator: 1e-02 Source power vs the EM dissipation: 1e-10 Whole-ball probe vs the volume mean: 1e-10

The test, not the blocks, computes the readings from the runs and checks them against these bands. A source twice as strong (the factor ½ of the time-averaged SAR dropped) misses the first band, and a probe ball moved 0.1 mm misses its own reading; the test runs both controls itself.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• A coil-driven source (MAT-15, WF-10).
  • A transient, a duty cycle or a container wall (duty_cycle_and_container_wall.md).
  • Perfusion.
  • Degree 2.
  • A CEM43 dose.
  • Tissue.
  • Any safety or compliance figure.
  • Any external-solver comparison.

docs.title: An implant rod in the coil-driven phantom
What you will compute
docs.text: The 4×4 S-matrix of the F-small birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1, 64 MHz) with a thin conducting rod inside its saline phantom, through a Study, and the 1 g mass-averaged SAR at the two rod tips. The rod is a hole in the mesh with a perfectly conducting wall. You will do it twice, from Python and from a study file, and both give the same S-matrix.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks. The Python block takes ≈ 2.5 min and the study file ≈ 1 min.

docs.title: Run it from Python
docs.text:
```python implant-rod from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

rod = {"radius": 1.0e-3, "length": 0.030, "centre": (0.015, 0.0, 0.0), "axis": (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)} study = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry(implant_rod=rod), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, ) result = study.solve() print(f"cells = {result.cells}")

tips = [(0.015, 0.0, 0.016), (0.015, 0.0, -0.016)] sar = study.sar(mass_g=1.0, centres=tips) print(sorted(sar), [len(per_centre) for per_centre in sar.values()])


`radius` and `length` are in metres, and `length` is the cylinder between the
centres of the two rounded caps. The two `tips` are the caps' apexes, 1 mm past
those centres. `Study.sar` is per 1 V drive, one entry per port.

## Run it from a study file

Save this as `implant_rod.yaml`:

```yaml implant-rod-file
femem: 1
study:
  frequency_hz: 64000000.0
  degree: 1
geometry:
  kind: four_port_birdcage
  preset: f_small
material:
  sigma: 0.5
  epsilon_r: 78.0
excitation:
  kind: lumped_port_drive
implant:
  rod:
    radius_m: 0.001
    length_m: 0.03
    centre_m: [0.015, 0.0, 0.0]
    axis: [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]

Then run it:

mpiexec -n 2 femem run implant_rod.yaml

The run writes a JSON summary carrying the S-matrix, and implant_rod.s4p, into femem_out/implant_rod/. All four rod keys are required. implant: is refused on any other geometry and beside load_result:, and the Palace backend refuses a rod.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
After the mesher's own output, at 2 ranks, the Python block prints:

```text implant-rod-expected cells = 168507


The cell count can change with the mesher's version. The S-matrix from the
Python block, from the study file, and from the fixture built directly without a
`Study` agree to this relative band:

```text implant-rod-bands
Python vs YAML vs the direct build: 1e-12

The test, not the block, computes these readings. The rod changes the S-matrix by far more than that band, and the test checks that too.

docs.title: With capacitor sheets
docs.text:
CapacitorSheets closes one port sheet with a series capacitor and its ESR — here sheet P2, 66.29 pF with 0.2 Ω — and the solve returns the 3×3 S-matrix of the other three ports. The rod is the same perfectly conducting rod as above, on the same mesh:

```python implant-rod-caps from fem_em_solver import CapacitorSheets, FourPortBirdcageGeometry, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

rod = {"radius": 1.0e-3, "length": 0.030, "centre": (0.015, 0.0, 0.0), "axis": (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)} study = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry(implant_rod=rod), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), CapacitorSheets(6.629e-11, esr_ohm=0.2, on=("P2",)), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, ) result = study.solve() print(f"cells = {result.cells}; ports = {[p.port_id for p in result.port_definitions]}")


At 2 ranks it prints:

```text implant-rod-caps-expected
cells = 168507; ports = ['P1', 'P3', 'P4']

Its 3×3 agrees with the same capacitor-terminated fixture built directly, without a Study, to this relative band:

```text implant-rod-caps-bands Python vs the direct build: 1e-12


This route is **degree 1 only**, and only `Study.solve` on the perfectly
conducting rod takes it. At degree 2 the same `Study` is refused before any
mesh:

```python implant-rod-caps-refused
from fem_em_solver import CapacitorSheets, FourPortBirdcageGeometry, Study
from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

rod = {"radius": 1.0e-3, "length": 0.030, "centre": (0.015, 0.0, 0.0), "axis": (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)}
study = Study(
    FourPortBirdcageGeometry(implant_rod=rod),
    GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6),
    CapacitorSheets(6.629e-11, esr_ohm=0.2, on=("P2",)),
    frequency_hz=64.0e6,
    degree=2,
)
study.solve()  # raises ValueError

The two refusals read, first at degree 2 and then on the copper hole route (as_hole=True with a LeontovichWall conductor):

```text implant-rod-caps-refusals solve: implant_rod at degree 2 is not gated; it needs degree 1 (WF-15 step 12) solve: implant_rod with CapacitorSheets is not gated (WF-15 step 12); only Study.solve on the PEC four-port at degree 1 is (WF-15 step 13)


## Heating the phantom around the rod

`Study.temperature` with `drive="P1"` heats the gel phantom with port `P1`
driven at 1 V on the rod `Study` above: the SAR of that one drive is the heat
source, the gel conducts it and cools through its outer boundary into air at
20 °C, and the rod's wall is adiabatic. It steps 40 Crank–Nicolson steps to
t\* = 1254 s and returns the volume mean and the 1 g ball means around the two
tips. Temperatures are rises above 20 °C, per watt dissipated in the
phantom: the block reads that power P from the EM solve and scales the heat
source by 1/P.

```python implant-rod-heating
from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, RobinCooling, Study, TransientSpec
from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial
from fem_em_solver.post.sar import mean_sar

rod = {"radius": 1.0e-3, "length": 0.030, "centre": (0.015, 0.0, 0.0), "axis": (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)}
study = Study(
    FourPortBirdcageGeometry(implant_rod=rod),
    GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6),
    LumpedPortDrive(),
    frequency_hz=64.0e6,
    degree=1,
)
transient = TransientSpec(dt_s=31.35, n_steps=40, rho_c_j_per_m3_k=4.18e6, theta=0.5,
                          startup_half_steps=2)
tips = [[0.015, 0.0, 0.016], [0.015, 0.0, -0.016]]
study.sar(mass_g=1.0, centres=tips, drives=["P1"])
fields = study.fields_result.fields["P1"]
P = mean_sar(fields.e_complex, sigma=fields.sigma_field, rho=study.density_kg_m3,
             cell_tags=study.fields_result.cell_tags,
             subdomain_ids=study.geometry.phantom_tag)["dissipated_power_w"]
cooling = RobinCooling(k_w_per_m_k=0.6, h_w_per_m2_k=10.0, t_inf_c=20.0, source_scale=1.0 / P)
heat = study.temperature(cooling, transient=transient, balls={"mass_g": 1.0, "centres": tips},
                         drive="P1")
print(f"cells = {heat.cells}")
for ball in heat.balls:
    print(ball["centre"], f"{ball['theta_k'][-1]:.6e} K")

The same run from the tracked study file tests/package/wf15/rod_heating.yaml, copied into the working directory. The tracked file omits thermal.source_scale, so as tracked it reads per 1 V on P1; add source_scale: <1/P> under thermal: to read per watt. The test runs exactly that copy with the Python block's P:

```python implant-rod-heating-file from fem_em_solver.study_yaml import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("rod_heating.yaml") for ball in run.summary["temperature"]["balls"]: print(ball["centre"], f"{ball['theta_k'][-1]:.6e} K")


The two blocks' tip temperatures at t\* agree, and the run's energy balance
and the volume heating slope of one backward-Euler step hold, to these bands:

```text implant-rod-heating-bands
Python vs the study file, tip temperature at t*: 1e-12
energy balance (E): 1e-09
volume slope (S2): 1e-04

The test, not the block, computes these readings, and checks each tip against the recorded value of the gated rod-heating test to its printed last digit.

docs.title: One step from the study file
docs.text:
The heating slopes are read from the study file too. rod_heating_step.yaml is the tracked file with the source_scale line added as above, and its transient: replaced by one backward-Euler step: dt_s: 0.0015675, n_steps: 1, theta: 1.0, startup_half_steps: 0. The block prints the volume mean rise and each tip ball's mean rise after that one step:

```python implant-rod-heating-step from fem_em_solver.study_yaml import run_study_file

run = run_study_file("rod_heating_step.yaml") t = run.summary["temperature"] print(f"volume mean {t['volume_mean_k'][1]:.6e} K") for ball in t["balls"]: print(ball["centre"], f"{ball['theta_k'][1]:.6e} K")


The test prints the step's tip and volume heating slopes beside the Python
route's one step (`study.temperature` with the same transient) and checks each
against the volume slope band above. Their agreement is printed, not gated: one
small step resolves the slopes only to the arithmetic of the step itself. The
study-file gate is the tip temperature at t\* from the file block above, which
the test checks equal to the Python route's to the identity band.

The rod file has no duty cycle: a `thermal.duty` key is refused as an unknown
key, and `Study.temperature(..., duty=...)` on the rod study raises
`ValueError`. [The malformed rod file](../../tests/package/wf15/malformed_rod_heating_duty.yaml)
carries one, and the check names that field and fails:

```bash implant-rod-heating-check
femem check malformed_rod_heating_duty.yaml

docs.title: What this does not tell you
docs.text:
• No two-port drive: every reading is one port driven at 1 V, so this is not the quadrature drive of a clinical coil.
  • No 1 g rung: the 1 g average is read on this one mesh, with no refined rung beside it.
  • No published comparand: the tip SAR, and its ratio to the same point with no rod, have no external value to agree with. The test prints the ratio as a reading with no record.
  • No tissue: the phantom is uniform saline, and the rod is a perfect conductor with no coating.
  • No other route: a rod Study at any degree but 1 is refused before any mesh, and so is a rod with CapacitorSheets anywhere but Study.solve on the perfectly conducting rod, because no test gates them. The capacitor section is not a tuned, rod-loaded coil, and the rod there is not copper. The heating section is degree 1, one port (P1) scaled to 1 W in the phantom, in gel, and makes no compliance claim.

docs.title: Temperature probes on the gel sphere from Python
What you will compute
docs.text:
The gelled-saline sphere in its air box (the MAT-12 fixture) is driven by the quasi-static uniform field and solved once. Its absorbed power heats the sphere under Robin cooling to the steady temperature rise θ = T − T∞. Four virtual probes then read the ball-averaged θ: one ball that encloses the whole sphere, and three small balls at the centre, off-axis, and near the surface. The whole-sphere ball must read the volume mean of θ, which is what the probe's quadrature is checked against.

This is the Python route of heating the gel sphere from YAML, whose probes section runs the same study from a file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build and 2 MPI ranks; the run takes ≈ 30 s. The steady temperature this route reuses is described on the temperature page.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
```python probe-python from fem_em_solver import QuasiStaticSphereField, RobinCooling, SphereInBoxGeometry, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial from fem_em_solver.thermal import ProbeBall

study = Study( SphereInBoxGeometry( sphere_radius=0.01, box_half_width=0.02, resolution_sphere=0.001, resolution_far=0.002, sphere_tag=1, ), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.57, 78.0, 64.0e6), QuasiStaticSphereField(e0=1.0), frequency_hz=64.0e6, density_kg_m3=1000.0, degree=1, ) result = study.solve() probes = [ ProbeBall((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.02), ProbeBall((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.002), ProbeBall((0.0035, 0.0, 0.0), 0.002), ProbeBall((0.0037527767497325675, 0.0037527767497325675, 0.0037527767497325675), 0.002), ] readings = study.probe(probes, RobinCooling(0.6, 100.0, 20.0, source_scale=25000000.0)) print(readings.values, readings.volumes)


`study.probe` reuses the solved field: it computes the steady temperature once
and averages θ over each ball on the mesh cells this rank owns.

## What you should see

The block prints one θ value (kelvin) and one mesh volume (m³) per probe. The
test compares them with these bands:

```text probe-python-bands
Whole-ball probe vs the volume mean: 1e-10
Displaced probe must miss by more than: 1e-09

The test computes the readings, not the block. The first line bounds the whole-sphere probe's value against ∫θ dx / V and its volume against V. The second line is the control: the third small probe moved 0.1 mm outward must read a different θ by more than that relative margin.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• A probe on a coil-driven field: the field here is imposed, not a birdcage's.
  • A transient or duty-cycled temperature (study.probe accepts transient and duty; this page does not run them).
  • Degree 2, a perfused tissue model, or a container wall.
  • The -n 1 against -n 2 width check, which the gate runs and this page does not.
  • Any statement against a commercial solver.

docs.title: The SAR-heated sphere over time, from one Study
What you will compute
docs.text:
The temperature rise of the 1 cm-radius gelled-saline sphere of the steady temperature page over time, heated by its own absorbed power q = G · ½σ|E|² from T(0) = T∞ = 0 and cooled through its surface (k = 0.6 W/(m·K), h = 100 W/(m²·K), G = 2.5e7). One Study solves the field once; two temperature(…, transient=TransientSpec(…)) calls then march the conduction equation on the sphere without a second field solve:

  • A: Crank–Nicolson (θ = 0.5, two backward-Euler half-steps first), 40 steps to t* = 0.2 R²ρc/k ≈ 139 s (Fourier number 0.2);
  • S: one backward-Euler step of dt₁ = 1e-5 R²ρc/k ≈ 7 ms — so short that the sphere has not yet conducted anything away, and the stored heat must equal the deposited heat (calorimetry).

Both results have a closed form: the Robin-cooled sphere's eigen-series at t*, and ρc·mean(θ) = dt₁·mean(q) for the single short step.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The fem-em-solver Docker service must be up (docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d), and you work inside it with the repository at /workspace.
  • The field solve is complex-valued: switch the container shell to the complex DolfinX build first with source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode.
  • Cost: ≈ 30 s wall time on 2 MPI ranks; "At the Study's default degree" costs ≈ 5 min and ≈ 21 GiB summed over 2 ranks.
  • Set degree=1 (except in "At the Study's default degree"). Study defaults to degree 2; the records below are the degree-1 ones.
  • T∞ = 0 here, so the temperature is the temperature rise θ.

docs.title: The study
docs.text:
```python sphere-transient from fem_em_solver import ( GelledSalinePhantomMaterial, QuasiStaticSphereField, RobinCooling, SphereInBoxGeometry, Study, TransientSpec, )

R = 0.01 # sphere radius, m k = 0.6 # W/(m K) rho_c = 1000.0 * 4180.0 # density x specific heat, J/(m^3 K) t_r = R**2 * rho_c / k # conduction time scale, s t_star = 0.2 * t_r # Fourier number 0.2 n_steps = 40 dt_1 = 1.0e-5 * t_r # the calorimetric step

geometry = SphereInBoxGeometry( sphere_radius=R, box_half_width=0.02, resolution_sphere=R / 10, resolution_far=R / 5, sphere_tag=1, ) material = GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.57, 78.0, 64e6) # sigma S/m, eps_r, Hz field = QuasiStaticSphereField(e0=1.0) # 1 V/m, along z

study = Study(geometry, material, field, frequency_hz=64e6, density_kg_m3=1000.0, degree=1) result = study.solve() # the one field solve cooling = RobinCooling(k, 100.0, 0.0, source_scale=2.5e7) # k, h, T_inf, G

heating = study.temperature(cooling, transient=TransientSpec(t_star / n_steps, n_steps, rho_c)) first_step = study.temperature( cooling, transient=TransientSpec(dt_1, 1, rho_c, theta=1.0, startup_half_steps=0) ) cells = heating.mesh.topology.index_map(3).size_global print(f"sphere cells = {cells}")


`heating.temperature` is θ(t*) (K) on the sphere, `heating.q` the heating
(W/m³), and `heating.max_balance_residual` the worst per-step energy-balance
residual; `first_step` carries the same fields for the single short step.

## Run it

Save the block as a Python script and run it inside the container, in complex
mode, on 2 ranks (`<script>` is the file you saved):

```bash
source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode
PYTHONPATH=/workspace/src mpiexec -n 2 python3 <script>

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
```text sphere-transient-output sphere cells = 19496 (A_t) 3.4708e-02 (S2) 4.9994e-05


The block prints the first line. The other two are what the test computes from
the block's results and must reproduce to four digits: **(A_t)** is the
interior relative L2 error of θ(t*) against the closed-form series (band 0.11),
and **(S2)** is |ρc·mean(θ) / (dt₁·mean(q)) − 1| after the single short step
(band 1e-04). The test also asserts the per-step energy balance of both runs to
≤ 1e-9 relative, and that the field was solved once.

## The same heating, pulsed

A `DutyCycle` switches the source on for the first half of each period
P = t\*/5 (8 steps) and off for the second. The block repeats the study above
and runs the continuous heating beside the pulsed one, both from the one field
solve:

```python sphere-transient-duty
from fem_em_solver import (
    DutyCycle,
    GelledSalinePhantomMaterial,
    QuasiStaticSphereField,
    RobinCooling,
    SphereInBoxGeometry,
    Study,
    TransientSpec,
)

R = 0.01  # sphere radius, m
k = 0.6  # W/(m K)
rho_c = 1000.0 * 4180.0  # density x specific heat, J/(m^3 K)
t_r = R**2 * rho_c / k  # conduction time scale, s
t_star = 0.2 * t_r  # Fourier number 0.2
n_steps = 40

geometry = SphereInBoxGeometry(
    sphere_radius=R,
    box_half_width=0.02,
    resolution_sphere=R / 10,
    resolution_far=R / 5,
    sphere_tag=1,
)
material = GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.57, 78.0, 64e6)  # sigma S/m, eps_r, Hz
field = QuasiStaticSphereField(e0=1.0)  # 1 V/m, along z

study = Study(geometry, material, field, frequency_hz=64e6, density_kg_m3=1000.0, degree=1)
result = study.solve()  # the one field solve
cooling = RobinCooling(k, 100.0, 0.0, source_scale=2.5e7)  # k, h, T_inf, G

dt = t_star / n_steps
heating = study.temperature(cooling, transient=TransientSpec(dt, n_steps, rho_c))
pulsed = study.temperature(cooling, transient=TransientSpec(dt, n_steps, rho_c), duty=DutyCycle(8 * dt, 0.5))
cells = heating.mesh.topology.index_map(3).size_global
print(f"sphere cells = {cells}")

pulsed.temperature is θ(t*) under the pulsed source, and pulsed.source_multipliers the on/off factor the march applied at each step. The switches fall on step boundaries, which is why the period is written as 8 * dt: a period that is not a whole number of steps would switch the source part-way through a step.

```text sphere-transient-duty-output sphere cells = 19496 (A_t) 3.4708e-02


The block prints the first line; the second is the continuous run's (A_t),
the record of "What you should see". The test checks the pulsed run against the
superposition of ten switched copies of the step-on run (Duhamel, `MAT-17`,
band 1e-12), and checks that it is *not* the continuous closed form.

## At the `Study`'s default degree

Leave `degree=` out and the `Study` solves the field with second-order
elements, its default; the heat equation stays first-order. The block is the
pulsed block above with that one keyword removed, and it prints the degree the
study used:

```python sphere-transient-degree2
from fem_em_solver import (
    DutyCycle,
    GelledSalinePhantomMaterial,
    QuasiStaticSphereField,
    RobinCooling,
    SphereInBoxGeometry,
    Study,
    TransientSpec,
)

R = 0.01  # sphere radius, m
k = 0.6  # W/(m K)
rho_c = 1000.0 * 4180.0  # density x specific heat, J/(m^3 K)
t_r = R**2 * rho_c / k  # conduction time scale, s
t_star = 0.2 * t_r  # Fourier number 0.2
n_steps = 40

geometry = SphereInBoxGeometry(
    sphere_radius=R,
    box_half_width=0.02,
    resolution_sphere=R / 10,
    resolution_far=R / 5,
    sphere_tag=1,
)
material = GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.57, 78.0, 64e6)  # sigma S/m, eps_r, Hz
field = QuasiStaticSphereField(e0=1.0)  # 1 V/m, along z

study = Study(geometry, material, field, frequency_hz=64e6, density_kg_m3=1000.0)
result = study.solve()  # the one field solve
cooling = RobinCooling(k, 100.0, 0.0, source_scale=2.5e7)  # k, h, T_inf, G

dt = t_star / n_steps
heating = study.temperature(cooling, transient=TransientSpec(dt, n_steps, rho_c))
pulsed = study.temperature(cooling, transient=TransientSpec(dt, n_steps, rho_c), duty=DutyCycle(8 * dt, 0.5))
cells = heating.mesh.topology.index_map(3).size_global
print(f"sphere cells = {cells}")
print(f"study degree = {study.degree}")

```text sphere-transient-degree2-output sphere cells = 19496 study degree = 2


The block prints both lines. The test checks the continuous run against the
same closed-form series and band (0.11) as "What you should see", the pulsed
run against the Duhamel superposition (band 1e-12), and that the pulsed run is
*not* the continuous closed form. This section costs ≈ 5 min wall time and
≈ 21 GiB of memory summed over 2 ranks.

## The same two runs from YAML files

The two runs are also shipped as study files:
[`sphere_mat12_transient_a.yaml`](../../tests/package/wf1/sphere_mat12_transient_a.yaml)
(run A) and
[`sphere_mat12_transient_s.yaml`](../../tests/package/wf1/sphere_mat12_transient_s.yaml)
(run S). Each carries the same sphere, field and cooling as the block above,
with `study.degree: 1` and T∞ = 0, and a `thermal.transient` mapping that
names the end time `t_end_s` and the step count `n_steps` (the step is
`t_end_s / n_steps`) beside ρc, θ and the startup half-steps. Each file is one
field solve and one transient, so the two runs below solve the field twice.

```python sphere-transient-yaml
from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

FILES = ["sphere_mat12_transient_a.yaml", "sphere_mat12_transient_s.yaml"]
runs = {name: run_study_file(name, output_dir=f"femem_out/{name[:-5]}") for name in FILES}
for name, run in runs.items():
    print(name, "cells", run.summary["cells"])

summary["cells"] counts the whole meshed box; run.thermal is the transient result on the sphere, with the same fields as heating and first_step above. The test computes (A_t) from the A run and (S2) from the S run and requires the records of "What you should see" to four digits.

A duty cycle has no key on this sphere: this file adds thermal.duty to the A file, and femem check exits with status 2 and names thermal.duty:

bash sphere-transient-yaml-check femem check malformed_sphere_transient_duty.yaml

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text: Degree 2 from Python only, with no degree-2 record on the page (its test asserts the bands), one duty schedule only (P = t*/5, D = 0.5, from Python; no periodic steady state), no perfusion, no probes, no tissue and no coil: the field is imposed on the box wall, and this is one mesh at degree 1. Study.probe is refused on this sphere with transient.

What you will compute

docs.title: Before you start

PYTHONPATH=/workspace/src mpiexec -n 2 python3 <script>

What you will compute

`femem check` reads a file without solving it. Three malformed files show
what a refusal looks like; each exits with status 2 and names the field it

`outputs.probes[1].radius`):

femem check malformed_thermal_box_probe_radius_zero.yaml
femem check malformed_thermal_ball_probe_radius_zero.yaml

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
The temperature rise against the closed-form series, as an interior relative error: the steady transverse-quadratic file, its Crank–Nicolson file at t*, and the duty-cycled transverse-quadratic file at t*. The test computes these from the runs (the series lives test-side); the blocks above only print the source class.

```text thermal-box-records steady transverse-quadratic interior error = 7.219878e-05 Crank-Nicolson transverse-quadratic interior error at t* = 2.694340e-04 duty-cycled transverse-quadratic interior error at t* = 2.543310e-04


## Start from a gradient, inside an acrylic wall

Two more files put the gel box inside a meshed acrylic wall
(`geometry.wall`: thickness, conductivity, volumetric heat capacity, and the
number of cells across it). The wall is on the top and bottom faces only
(the z faces): the box's four side faces are insulated, and the Robin cooling
acts on the outer faces of the wall alone. One file also starts the gel from a
linear profile in z (`thermal.initial.gradient_k_per_m`) instead of a uniform
temperature; the other is the same file without `initial`, starting uniform.

```python thermal-box-wall-gradient
from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

FILES = ["thermal_box_wall_gradient_m4.yaml", "thermal_box_wall_m4.yaml"]
runs = {name: run_study_file(name, output_dir=f"femem_out/{name[:-5]}") for name in FILES}
for name, run in runs.items():
    print(name, run.summary["temperature"].get("initial_gradient_k_per_m"))

The gradient file's summary carries initial_gradient_k_per_m; the uniform file's does not, so the block prints None for it.

A wall needs its thickness. This file leaves it out; femem check exits with status 2 and names geometry.wall.thickness_m:

```bash thermal-box-wall-check femem check malformed_thermal_box_wall_without_thickness.yaml


The test reads the gradient run's temperature at one gel point and checks it
equals a direct solve of the same walled box, built and solved without the
YAML layer; the uniform file's reading misses it by the recorded effect of
the initial profile.

## Read the thermal dose at two points

Two more files are the walled-box files above with a `thermal.dose` section
added: [thermal_box_wall_gradient_m4_dose.yaml](../../tests/package/wf1/thermal_box_wall_gradient_m4_dose.yaml)
starts from the gradient and
[thermal_box_wall_m4_dose.yaml](../../tests/package/wf1/thermal_box_wall_m4_dose.yaml)
starts uniform. `thermal.dose.points_m` lists the gel points whose
temperature history is read at every time step, and `window_s` sets the
trailing window of the running mean (six minutes when omitted). The run's
summary then carries a `dose` entry: for each point, `cem43_s` is `MAT-20`'s
∫ R^(43 − T) dt over the history, in seconds (divide by 60 for CEM43
minutes), beside the peak of the trailing-window mean.

```python thermal-box-dose
from fem_em_solver import run_study_file

FILES = ["thermal_box_wall_gradient_m4_dose.yaml", "thermal_box_wall_m4_dose.yaml"]
runs = {name: run_study_file(name, output_dir=f"femem_out/{name[:-5]}") for name in FILES}
for name, run in runs.items():
    print(name, run.summary["dose"]["points_m"])

The dose is read on the walled files only, and never beside a duty cycle. A dose section needs the wall; this file leaves out its thickness, and femem check exits with status 2 and names geometry.wall.thickness_m:

bash thermal-box-dose-check femem check malformed_thermal_box_dose_wall_without_thickness.yaml

The test checks the gradient run's dose at both points against the dose of a direct solve of the same walled box, and checks each history's dose and trailing mean against a quadrature of the same samples; the uniform file's dose misses the gradient file's at the first point. There is no dose limit, no damage threshold and no compliance statement here: cem43_s is a number read off a temperature history, nothing more.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text: No electromagnetic solve, coil or SAR; no perfusion; P2 for the quadratic files and the uniform P2 file, P1 for the others; m = 4 and m = 6 meshes only, so no h-statement. The probe readings are real-build records and are only printed beside a complex-build run here. The dose section reads CEM43 on the walled files only: no dose limit or threshold, no dose under a duty cycle or beside probes, no compliance statement, and no external-solver comparison.

docs.title: What you will compute
docs.text:
The 10 g mass-averaged SAR at one point in the gel phantom of the human-scale 16-leg copper birdcage, tuned at 64 MHz and driven in quadrature from two feeds. Every one of the 32 leg gaps carries a lumped capacitor with a 0.2 Ω series resistance, modelled as a sheet whose impedance is Z = r + 1/(jωC); the resistance is where part of the drive power is lost outside the phantom and the copper.

The copper is not meshed: the coil is cut out of the air and its surface is a Leontovich (surface-impedance) wall. The two feeds sit 90° apart and are driven with weights (1, -1j) — the co-rotating (ccw) sense. A two-feed drive keeps exactly one mirror of the coil, the plane bisecting the two feeds, so the readout point sits on a feed azimuth rather than on that plane.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The complex DolfinX build: source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode.
  • 8 MPI ranks, ≈ 3–4 min.
  • degree=1 is set explicitly. The Study default is degree 2, which this coil cannot afford at this width.

docs.title: The study
docs.text:
```python tuned-copper-birdcage import numpy as np

from fem_em_solver import ( FHumanBirdcageGeometry, GelledSalinePhantomMaterial, LeontovichWall, Study, TwoPortQuadratureDrive, )

geometry = FHumanBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True) # copper coil cut out of the air phantom = GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64e6) # sigma S/m, eps_r, Hz c_in = 118.2437 * 1e-12 # the in-model Larmor capacitance on copper, F drive = TwoPortQuadratureDrive(c_in, esr_ohm=0.2) # 0.2 ohm ESR on every gap

study = Study(geometry, phantom, drive, frequency_hz=64e6, conductor=LeontovichWall(), degree=1) az = np.radians(11.25) # the P17 feed azimuth c_star = (0.045 * np.cos(az), 0.045 * np.sin(az), 0.0) # r = 45 mm, mid-plane sar = study.sar(mass_g=10.0, centres=[c_star], drives=("ccw",)) print(f"SAR10g(c*) = {sar['ccw'][0]['averaged_sar_w_per_kg']:.4e} W/kg")


## Run it

Save the block as a Python script and run it inside the container, in complex
mode, on 8 ranks (`<script>` is the file you saved):

```bash
source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode
PYTHONPATH=/workspace/src mpiexec -n 8 python3 <script>

docs.text: No tuning-accuracy, f₀, Q or match claim; no compliance or absolute SAR claim (the figure is per the package's unit drive). c* is the argmax of a fixed lattice of ball centres, not a global SAR maximum. Degree 1 only.

docs.title: The tuned copper birdcage from a YAML file
What you will compute
docs.text:
The same coil as the tuned copper birdcage — the human-scale 16-leg copper birdcage, tuned at 64 MHz, a 0.2 Ω series resistance on every one of its 32 capacitor gaps, driven from two feeds 90° apart — but described in a study file instead of Python. femem run (or run_study_file from Python) solves the file once and writes a JSON summary holding the node S-matrix, the active admittances Y_in for each sense of rotation, the 10 g mass-averaged SAR at 19 ball centres, and |B₁⁺| at two points.

The first 18 centres are a fixed lattice in the phantom (three radii, four azimuths at the mid-plane, and two off-plane rows). The 19th centre is the image of the lattice's hottest point c* under the plane bisecting the two feeds: that mirror maps the feed azimuth 11.25° onto 101.25°, so it lands exactly on lattice row 6 (r = 45 mm, a quarter turn from c*). It is not an independent centre; it is listed so that the summary carries the counter-rotating (cw) reading at the mirror image of c* beside c*'s co-rotating (ccw) one.

docs.text:
• The complex DolfinX build: source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode.

docs.title: Tuning a saved human-scale result: the 32-port birdcage with no second solve
What you will compute
docs.text:
The mode capacitance C_mode of the tuned copper F-human birdcage (32 ring-gap ports, Leontovich copper rings and legs, degree 1) around its saline phantom, read from a 32×32 S-matrix that was solved once and saved to a Touchstone file. A fresh Study with the same inputs reads that file with Study.load_result and calls Study.tune(1, n_slots=16) on it. The fresh Study never solves: tune runs on the loaded matrix.

This is Tuning a saved result at human scale: the solve needs the mesh, the tune needs only the S-matrix.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 8 MPI ranks; the block below takes ≈ 4 minutes, nearly all of it the one solve. This is a heavy run. It writes the Touchstone file f_human_cu_64mhz.s32p into the directory you run it from.

docs.title: Solve once, save, then tune the saved file
docs.text:
```python loaded-tune-human from fem_em_solver import FHumanBirdcageGeometry, LeontovichWall, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial from fem_em_solver.study import COPPER_SIGMA

def f_human_study(): return Study( FHumanBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), conductor=LeontovichWall(COPPER_SIGMA), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, )

docs.title: Solve once and save the 32x32 S-matrix.
docs.text: solved = f_human_study() result = solved.solve() path = result.write_touchstone("f_human_cu_64mhz.s32p")

docs.title: Later, or in another session: a fresh Study reads the file and tunes it.
docs.text:
fresh = f_human_study() fresh.load_result(path) tuned = fresh.tune(1, n_slots=16) print(f"k = {tuned.k}, C_mode = {tuned.c_mode_farad:.4e} F")


On this ring `load_result` reads a file holding exactly one frequency, equal
to the Study's own (a multi-frequency file loads on the four-port only), and
one port per ring gap (32 here); any other file is refused before anything is
stored. The ring tune reads the port names from the file.
A loaded result carries an S-matrix and nothing else, so the field reads
(`sar`, `b1_plus`, `temperature`) raise `TypeError` on it.

## What you should see

The block prints the mode-1 capacitance. It matches the capacitance the same
Study gives when it is tuned straight after its own solve, to the band below:

```text loaded-tune-human-bands
Saved-file C_mode vs the solved-Study record: 1e-03

The test, not the block, computes the reading and checks it against this band.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• A resonance, match, Q or R_in statement: C_mode is a lossless circuit-model read of one solve.
  • The same load from a study file through femem run.
  • A 64-port (F-clinical) file, or any field computed from a loaded file.
  • Degree 2.
  • Any external-solver comparison.

docs.text: tests/package/test_wf17_loaded_tune_human_tutorial.py execs the tagged block at 8 ranks in the complex build, checks that it solves exactly once and that the fresh Study never solves, compares its capacitance to the recorded one at the band above, and checks that the same file with ports 1 and 2 swapped misses it.

docs.title: Tuning a saved result: the mode capacitance with no second solve
What you will compute
docs.text:
The mode capacitance C_mode of the four-port F-small birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1, perfectly conducting rings and legs cut out of the mesh) around its saline phantom, read from a 4×4 S-matrix that was solved once and saved to a Touchstone file. A fresh Study with the same inputs reads that file with Study.load_result and calls Study.tune(1) on it. The fresh Study never solves: tune runs on the loaded matrix.

This is the same read as Tuning a study, split in two: the solve, which needs the mesh, and the tune, which needs only the S-matrix. The same tune from a study file through femem run is Tuning a saved result from a YAML file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks; the block below takes ≈ 1 min, nearly all of it the one solve. It writes the Touchstone file into the directory you run it from.

docs.title: Solve once, save, then tune the saved file
docs.text:
```python loaded-tune from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

def f_small_study(): return Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True, strip_fraction=0.5), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, )

docs.title: Solve once and save the 4x4 S-matrix.
docs.text: solved = f_small_study() result = solved.solve() path = result.write_touchstone("f_small_pec_64mhz.s4p")

docs.title: Later, or in another session: a fresh Study reads the file and tunes it.
docs.text:
fresh = f_small_study() fresh.load_result(path) tuned = fresh.tune(1) print(f"k = {tuned.k}, C_mode = {tuned.c_mode_farad:.4e} F")


`load_result` reads a file holding one frequency equal to the Study's own, or
several whose span contains it, and as many ports as the birdcage has legs;
any other file is refused before anything is stored. On a multi-frequency
file, `tune` needs `at_hz`: it picks the file's nearest frequency, with no
interpolation, and refuses a value outside the span. It is defined on a four-port Study driven
by `LumpedPortDrive` only. A loaded result carries an S-matrix and nothing
else, so the field reads (`sar`, `b1_plus`, `b1_plus_at`) raise `TypeError` on
it, naming `load_result`.

## What you should see

The block prints the mode-1 capacitance. It matches the capacitance the same
Study gives when it is tuned straight after its own solve, to the band below:

```text loaded-tune-bands
Saved-file C_mode vs the solved-Study record: 1e-03

The test, not the block, computes the reading and checks it against this band.

docs.title: A file holding several frequencies
docs.text:
A Touchstone file can hold a sweep. A frequency sweep from YAML writes one from f_small_sweep.yaml: produce your own that way and name it f_small_sweep.s4p. This repository does not carry the file. From there on nothing is meshed or solved, so each route below takes about a second. tune needs at_hz on such a file, and the capacitance is read with the selected frequency's own ω.

```python swept-tune from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

study = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True, strip_fraction=0.5), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, ) study.load_result("f_small_sweep.s4p") rows = [study.tune(1, at_hz=f) for f in (1.0e7, 6.4e7, 1.28e8)] for tuned in rows: c = float(tuned.c_mode_farad) print(f"{tuned.frequency_hz:.6e} Hz: C_mode = {c:.6e} F ({c.hex()})")


The same read from a study file, next to the Touchstone file, is one
`at_hz` per file. Run it with `mpiexec -n 2 femem run <file> --output-dir <dir>`;
the `tune` block of the summary in that directory holds the selected
`frequency_hz` and `c_mode_farad`.

```yaml swept-tune-file
femem: 1
study:
  frequency_hz: 64000000.0
  degree: 1
geometry:
  kind: four_port_birdcage
  preset: f_small
  as_hole: true
material:
  sigma: 0.5
  epsilon_r: 78.0
excitation:
  kind: lumped_port_drive
load_result: f_small_sweep.s4p
tune:
  k: 1
  at_hz: 64000000.0

On U71's sweep file, both routes give these three lines, the block by printing them and the study file through its summary at each at_hz. The hexadecimal figure is the exact value:

```text swept-tune-lines 1.000000e+07 Hz: C_mode = 2.472676e-09 F (0x1.53d78952a75e9p-29) 6.400000e+07 Hz: C_mode = 6.166035e-11 F (0x1.0f2f6316ff1dep-34) 1.280000e+08 Hz: C_mode = 1.513381e-11 F (0x1.0a3c9bbb69f6ep-36)


Each value matches the single-frequency tune of the same column to the band

Swept-file C_mode vs the single-frequency tune of its column: 1e-03

tune selects the file's nearest frequency and never interpolates between two of them. An at_hz outside the file's span is refused: tune raises ValueError, and femem run refuses the field tune.at_hz, exits with status 2 and writes no output directory. tune with no at_hz raises ValueError naming at_hz. femem run with no tune.at_hz on a swept file refuses that field with status 2.

docs.title: The human-scale birdcage
docs.text:
On the tuned copper F-human birdcage (32 ring-gap ports, Leontovich copper) the tune reads the ring mode with n_slots=16. load_result accepts this Study since WF-16 step 15 (a 32-port Touchstone file, one per ring-gap port, tuned with n_slots=16); the block below still solves first and tunes the solved Study:

from fem_em_solver import FHumanBirdcageGeometry, LeontovichWall, LumpedPortDrive, Study
from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial
from fem_em_solver.study import COPPER_SIGMA

study = Study(
    FHumanBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True),
    GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6),
    LumpedPortDrive(),
    conductor=LeontovichWall(COPPER_SIGMA),
    frequency_hz=64.0e6,
    degree=1,
)
tuned = study.tune(1, n_slots=16)

This block is not run by this page's test: it is a heavy solve. Its recorded reading is 1.181185799070e-10 F, at 8 ranks, logged at docs/testing/logs/20261015T213534Z_WF-16-s12-W1.log.gz line 7375 and quoted at tests/package/test_wf1_yaml_tune_f_human.py lines 75–76.

  • A saved human-scale file holding several frequencies: it is refused.

docs.title: Tuning a saved result from a YAML file
What you will compute
docs.text:
The mode capacitance C_mode of the four-port F-small birdcage (exact port rectangles, κ off, degree 1, perfectly conducting rings and legs cut out of the mesh) around its saline phantom, read by femem run from a 4×4 S-matrix that was solved once and saved to a Touchstone file. The study file names that file under a top-level load_result: key beside its tune: section, so femem run calls Study.load_result and Study.tune(1) and never meshes or solves.

This is Tuning a saved result with the second half moved into a study file, and Tuning from a YAML file with the solve replaced by a saved file.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need the complex DolfinX build (source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode) and 2 MPI ranks. The first step takes ≈ 1 min, nearly all of it the one solve; the second takes about a second. Run every step from the same directory.

docs.title: Step 1: solve once and save the S-matrix
docs.text:
Run this block as a Python script on 2 ranks. It writes f_small_pec_64mhz.s4p into the directory you run it from.

```python loaded-yaml-solve from fem_em_solver import FourPortBirdcageGeometry, LumpedPortDrive, Study from fem_em_solver.materials import GelledSalinePhantomMaterial

solved = Study( FourPortBirdcageGeometry(as_hole=True, strip_fraction=0.5), GelledSalinePhantomMaterial(0.5, 78.0, 64.0e6), LumpedPortDrive(), frequency_hz=64.0e6, degree=1, ) result = solved.solve() path = result.write_touchstone("f_small_pec_64mhz.s4p") print(f"wrote {path}")


## Step 2: the study file

Save this as `f_small_pec_load.yaml` in the same directory. It is
[`f_small_hole_pec_tune.yaml`](../../tests/package/wf1/f_small_hole_pec_tune.yaml)
(the study of step 1, plus `tune: {k: 1}`) with one line added, `load_result:`.

```yaml loaded-yaml-file
femem: 1
study:
  frequency_hz: 64000000.0
  degree: 1
geometry:
  kind: four_port_birdcage
  preset: f_small
  as_hole: true
material:
  sigma: 0.5
  epsilon_r: 78.0
excitation:
  kind: lumped_port_drive
load_result: f_small_pec_64mhz.s4p
tune:
  k: 1

The study sections must still be there: load_result reads a file with four ports, one per leg, holding one frequency equal to study.frequency_hz or several frequencies. A file holding several needs tune.at_hz; without it run_study_file stops with a ValueError naming at_hz, and femem run refuses the field tune.at_hz with status 2. A relative load_result: path is resolved against the directory of the YAML file, not the directory you run from.

load_result: is defined on a four_port_birdcage, an f_clinical_birdcage or an f_human_birdcage, with excitation.kind: lumped_port_drive only, and it needs a tune: section. A loaded result has an S-matrix and no fields, so conductor, thermal, study.sweep_hz and the field outputs (sar, b1_plus, probes) are refused when the file is parsed, each by name. conductor is admitted on an f_human_birdcage alone, where it records what the saved file was solved with and nothing is solved.

docs.title: Step 3: check and run it
docs.text:
```bash loaded-yaml-cli source /usr/local/bin/dolfinx-complex-mode mpiexec -n 2 femem check f_small_pec_load.yaml mpiexec -n 2 femem run f_small_pec_load.yaml --output-dir femem_out


`femem check` prints the resolved path of the saved file, so you can see
which file the run will read before it runs. With the directory you work in
in place of `/your/work/dir`, its `load_result` line is:

```text loaded-yaml-check
load_result: '/your/work/dir/f_small_pec_64mhz.s4p'

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
The run's JSON summary, written into femem_out, carries the same tune block the solve route writes (its keys are listed on Tuning from a YAML file), plus load_result, the resolved path that was read. It carries no cells and no touchstone: nothing was meshed or solved. Its c_mode_farad matches the capacitance the solved Study gives when it is tuned straight after its own solve, to the band below:

text loaded-yaml-bands Saved-file C_mode from femem run vs the solved-Study record: 1e-09

The test, not the page, computes the reading and checks it against this band.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
• A resonance, match, Q or R_in statement: C_mode is a lossless circuit-model read of one solve.
  • Loading a saved human-scale (32-port) result: Tuning a saved human-scale result.
  • Any field output (SAR, B1+, probes) from a loaded file; these are refused by design.
  • A worked file holding several frequencies: A file holding several frequencies.
  • Degree 2, or the copper (Leontovich) rings on F-small.
  • Any external-solver comparison.
